en: The Procedure for the Western Worship:
Victory to the Lord of the Three Worlds, the Supreme Self of the ninefold nature!
Victory to the omnipresent Goddess; salutations to her who is established upon the head!
Śrī 3 Bhavānīśaṅkara (1a) 1. Oṃ, salutation to the glorious Navātman.
He who arises as the sixteen-fold self in the lunar [wheel] from a body established in the essence of nectar, and who,
moving by means of a portion of power in the solar [wheel], shines forth as both the manifest and the unmanifest through twelve parts;
he, whose nature is the light of prāṇa and apāna, [resides] in the wheels called the Sun and the Moon by means of the digits of the quarters and the seasons.
I bow to that illustrious Navanātha, the Lord of the Śrīkrama, who is established as the glory of the Krama and Kula traditions.
Having prostrated at the lotus feet of my Guru, the illustrious Sahadeva, I, Śrī Vimalaprabodha, [shall compose] the manual for the Western worship (paścimārcanapaddhati).
Having heard the speech of the illustrious Śambhu as it issued from the mouth of the true teacher,
[he shall explain] for the benefit of his disciples the threefold [system] clearly and in brief.
Requested by a disciple who was endowed with the performance of daily, occasional, and optional worship, and who possessed a mind fixed on Śambhu through the practice of full residence (pūrṇāvāsa),
[the teacher] first rose from his bed at dawn during the transit of Saturn, while performing inhalation (pūraka); having meditated upon and saluted the Guru, he sat upon another seat facing westward.

Having sat in the *svastika* posture, one should contemplate the *kuṭa* within one's own heart according to the sequence to be described; then, having performed the threefold ritual placement (*nyāsa*) consisting of the Goddess, the six messengers (*ṣaḍdūtī*), and the *trikhaṇḍikā*, and having offered the fourfold oblations (*bali*) beginning with the *śānti* offering, one should perform the necessary duties (*āvaśyaka*). In the event of incapacity, one should simply remember the Guru and the Deity from one's bed.

Having risen, one should perform the daily rites (*nityakarman*) according to the prescribed rule. Having completed the bath and other preliminaries, one should stand facing the Guru and perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the *praṇavas* (syllables *oṃ*) in both direct and reverse order: from the youngest to the eldest, and from the eldest to the youngest; from the base (*ādhāra*) to the throat, and from the head to the anus. Then, kneeling on the ground, one should form a square mandala with those very [syllables] and, restraining it with the right thumb, [place them]: *eṃ* in the southeast (*vahni*), *hrīṃ* in the northeast (*īśa*), *śrīṃ* in the southwest (*nairṛtya*), *hsphreṃ* in the northwest (*vāma*), and *hsauṃ*.

(2b) In the center. Having offered a flower with this [mantra]: *hraṃ amukānandanāthagurave amukā parāvvā hraṃ 5 pā pū*. Having thus worshipped the pair of feet of the manifest guru three times, and having knelt with knees and elbows on the ground, one should fill the hands in añjali with flowers. *5*
"O Great Lord, O Śrī Guru, you who wear the nine-fold wick [of the lamp], please instruct me on the sequence for the daily rites, preceded by your own worship.
Having thus requested permission and performed a mental prostration, one should smell a flower and cast it away. In the case of a Guru residing in another land, one should face that direction.

Having prepared the mandala and so forth according to the stated sequence, and having meditated upon his form, one should worship the deity with the heart-mantra and offer the bracelets to the Guru. In the case where the Guru is situated in another world, one should face west, meditate on the form of the Navātman, and [offer] the water for the feet and other items according to the sequence to be described.

Having given [the offerings] and worshipped, one should place the abode of the deity within one's own heart; then, having received the command of the Guru, one should assume the lotus posture (padmāsana), perform inhalation (pūraka) through the left nostril, and having formed the tortoise gesture (kamaṭhamudrā), by means of breath retention (kumbhaka), one should [visualize] within the heart—

in the center of the pericarp of a white eight-petaled lotus— the peak of the deity (devakūṭa) according to the oral instruction, resembling a stainless autumn moon and having the form of a lamp flame.

Having led [the breath] to the end of the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus situated at the *brahmarandhra*, and having meditated there upon the raining down of thousands of streams of cool nectar, one should, at the moment of exhalation (*recaka*), make that very peak the abode of its crest; then, having contemplated the Self as pure white and having placed water in the right hand—

With the left fingers, [reciting] *lā vā rā yā hā sā* five times, one should consecrate that water seven times with this mantra. By means of the *chaṭā*-gesture, one should perform an ablution three times upon the head; the remaining water should be placed in another vessel containing water. This is the *mantra-snāna*.
Now, having drawn a circular mandala with the syllable *Oṃ*, one should place upon it a *viśvāmitra-kāṃsya* vessel filled with water mixed with flowers and meat offerings (*sāmiṣa*).

Having placed one of the new earthen vessels upon it and having performed the *pūraka* and *kumbhaka* breath-retentions as before, one should unify the mass of rays— yellow, dark-blue, red, smoke-colored, white, and deep-red— which reside in the anus, navel, genitals, heart, throat, and between the eyebrows by means of the syllable *Oṃ*, [and dissolve them] into the lotus of the heart.

Having established [the deity] with the syllable *hrīṃ*, one should mentally rotate the sixteen-syllable mantra to be described three times. Then, by means of the "flowing" (*vahatpuṭa*) breath-retention, one should unite that sphere of rays within the vessel. From that arises [the deity]: white, with three red circular eyes, tawny hair standing upright, laughing with a loud *aṭṭaṭṭa* laugh, two-armed, holding a skull-cup in the right hand and the *tarpaṇa* mudrā in the left, wearing a garland of severed heads, short-statured, pot-bellied, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, clad in a tiger skin, and seated upon a red lotus.

Having meditated upon [the deity] seated upon a skull-cup filled with blood, encircled by five rays of light—yellow, dark green, red, smoky, and white—or having meditated upon the corpse of all beings colored according to the five elements, [one recites]: Oṃ hrīḥ, to all obstructing spirits and to all beings, hrāḥ svāhā.

Having turned [the vessel] three times in a low voice, having displayed the left index finger, and having offered the oblation (*bali*) with a red flower, one should snap the fingers three times with the right hand.

Meditating upon that *bali*-person in the form of a white drop (*bindu*) by means of the syllable *oṃ*, one should cause that drop to dissolve into one's own heart through inhalation (*pūraka*) and the withdrawal gesture (*saṃhāramudrā*) while reciting the Heart-mantra of the Deity. Then, one should place that *bali* in an impure location using the seven-step movement; this is the *śānti-bali*.
Then, when there is the capacity [for this], having likewise constructed the maṇḍala and arranged the vessel, one should meditate on a second red [syllable] at the navel;

having emitted its rays as drops through the nostrils, one should visualize the blood arising from that, having the form of a sixteen-year-old, with three crests, and adorned with the ornaments of a youth.

Having meditated upon [the deity] mounted on a golden sandal, two-armed and three-eyed, holding a golden staff in the left hand and a skull-cup in the right, one should offer: *hrīṃ kulavaṭukāya hrīṃ baliṃ gṛhāṇa svāhā* (five times).

Having offered in that same manner and likewise displayed the mudrā, one should dissolve [the deity] into the heart of the god at the navel; then, in the same way, one should give [the offering]. Again, in the same manner, having placed the vessel in the maṇḍala...

At the time of destruction, O Nṛsiṃha, having meditated upon Kapila and likewise expelled him, one should visualize [the deity] born from that— dwarfish, pot-bellied, naked, with tawny, wide-spreading hair,
adorned with a girdle of a network of small bells, holding a chopper, a skull-cup, and a *khaṭvāṅga*, and with his hand placed upon a skull resting atop the *khaṭvāṅga* above his left breast.
Having meditated upon the black *maṭakā* seat in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, one should offer [the oblation] while reciting: *kṣrūaṃ kulakṣetrapālāya kṣrūaṃ baliṃ gṛhāṇa svāhā* (five times).

Having likewise brought [the deity] into dissolution, one should give [the offering]. Again, having established the maṇḍala vessel in the same manner and having meditated upon yellow *yeluka* on a golden leaf, one should likewise extract [the deity] with the index finger acting as a *kuśa* grass; [one visualizes the deity] three-eyed, with sunken eyes (*koṭarākṣa*), with a tawny matted lock, standing in the *vaiśākha* stance, mounted upon a skeleton, and adorned with fierce ornaments.

Having meditated on [the deity] whose shoulder bears a vajra-hammer and red arsenic (*sajjikā*), holding a skull-cup in the right hand, one recites: *lūṃ laḥ kulaceṭakāya hraḥ laḥ baliṃ gṛhāṇa svāhā* five times.

Having thus offered [the oblation], one should dismiss [the deity] in the same manner. It should be explained that for these—Vaṭuka, Kṣetrapāla, and Ceṭaka—a special worship and so forth must be performed at the time of purification (*sodhana*).
The fourfold offering of the *śānti* and other rites.

Now, having fashioned a square mandala with a circle in its center using the *praṇavas*, one should place a flower in its middle while reciting "hsauṃ" five times. Thereafter, through the practice of breath-retention (*kumbhaka*), one should meditate on the yellow-colored seed-syllable "hrāṃ" at the anus; then, by means of exhalation (*recaka*) through the *vahat-nāḍī*, it is drawn out and placed upon the pericarp of a red eight-petaled lotus situated in the sky.

Having established her with a handful of flowers, one should visualize her arising therefrom: yellow in color, three-eyed, adorned with a mass of matted hair and a crescent moon, four-armed, with her right hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and her left hands holding a skull-cup and a snake;
adorned with jewels, gold, and other ornaments, having the form of a sixteen-year-old, graceful, wearing a forest garland, and situated in the center of a solar disc.

Having meditated on [the deity] as red in color, two-armed, holding a pair of white lotuses, adorned with red ornaments, wearing a crown and earrings, with the head slightly tilted upward, and seated upon a solar throne—one should worship three times with: *5 hlā̃ hsaũ hlāṃ 5 jyeṣṭhāyai pā pū*. Then, with either *5 hlā̃ hsõ hlāṃ jyeṣṭhāyai hlā̃ hsaũ hlāṃ 5* or *hlāṃ jyeṣṭhāyai atraṃ hlāṃ 5*, one should likewise offer flowers, incense, lamps, water for rinsing the mouth, food offerings, and water for rinsing the mouth.

One should offer betel leaves and so forth. In the absence of these nine items, one should satisfy [the deity] three times with the root mantra, worship it again three times, and satisfy it once more. Then, having displayed the *yonimudrā* with its seed-syllable (*bīja*), and having performed recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity, one should offer a flower with the root mantra. With the *yonimudrā*, one should lead the deity—whose form is that of the seed-syllable—from its own place into the abode of the heart by means of the heart-mantra. This is the morning twilight ritual (*prātaḥsaṃdhyā*).

Then, having constructed the maṇḍala as before, one should visualize a dark seed-syllable *hvī̃* at the navel; having likewise projected it forth and established it, one should [visualize] the goddess arising from that— dark in color,

adorned with the ornaments of the previously mentioned twilight-form, holding a rosary and a book, situated in the center of a moon-maṇḍala, adorned with white ornaments, and holding two white water-lilies.

The remainder is like that of the Sun. Having thus meditated upon her seated on a lunar throne, one should worship three times with: *hvīṃ hsauṃ hvīṃ* (five times) and *vāmāyai pā pū*. Then, one should perform everything according to the previously mentioned sequence of the twilight rites using one's own seed-syllable (*svabīja*); this is the midday twilight rite (*madhyāhnasaṃdhyā*).

Now, having prepared the maṇḍala according to the stated sequence, one should contemplate the red [deity] at the *liṅga* with the syllable *hrūṃ*, and likewise, having extracted and established her, one should contemplate the red Muṇḍamālinī born from that.

[One should meditate on her] holding a trident, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a skull-cup (*kapāla*), and a threatening finger (*tarjanī*), adorned with fierce ornaments, and situated in the midst of a circle of fire. Having recited the red [seed-syllable], one should meditate on the one who holds a spear (*śakti*), who has black, long-crested hair, a protruding belly, and the rest as [described for] the Sun. Having thus meditated upon her seated upon fire, one should worship three times with: *hrūṃ auṃ hsauṃ hrūṃ auṃ* five times, and *raudryai pā pū*. Then, as before, [perform] everything.
"One should perform [this]" refers to the evening twilight (*sāyaṃsaṃdhyā*).

Now, having constructed the mandala at night according to the previously described sequence, one should extract from the heart the seven-piṇḍa red [deity] as before and establish it there. [One should visualize her] as black, three-eyed, with a face terrifying with fangs, with tawny hair standing upright in matted locks, adorned with the ornaments of Bhairava, holding a sword and a chopper in the right hand, and holding a skull-bowl containing a fair-skinned [head] and a beard in the left.

Having meditated upon her situated in the center of the mandala—smoky-colored, most beautiful, adorned with ornaments, two-armed, holding a banner in her left hand, and likewise seated upon the elements and wind—one should worship her according to the previously mentioned sequence with "Hskhphrāṃ" five times, "Niśāyai," "Hskhphrāṃ" five times, and "Pā Pū. Then, one should cause her to dissolve into her own place; this is the evening twilight ritual (*niśā-sandhyā*).
According to another view, one should worship at the tip of the nose through the sequence of time and by means of instruction; this is the fourfold worship of the *saṃdhyā*s.
Now, an offering of water (*jalāñjali*) to Navātmānandanātha: 5.5. An offering of water to Samayāparāmbā: 5.
Likewise [offerings] to Maṅgalamahābhairava, Brahmāṇī, Cakreśvarī, Māheśvarī, Yoginī, Kaumārī, Harasiddhavaiṣṇavī, Bhaṭṭavārāhī, Kila Kila, and Indrāṇī.

Having satiated Kālarātri, Cāmuṇḍā, Bhīṣaṇā, and Mahālakṣmī according to the stated order [with five offerings], one should again satisfy all the gurus with five [offerings], all the ancestors with five [offerings], and various others with a single recitation as follows: "I satisfy the venerable Navātman, Navātmikā, the Guru, the Pitṛs, the Kṣetras, the Siddhas, the Grahas, and the Analas."
5. Thus, having recited the *saṃtarpaṇa* mantras, one should dissolve them into the heart; this is the procedure for the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
Now, with the seed-syllable *hrāṃ*, one should draw an eight-petalled red lotus within a square mandala, and below that, a square mandala for the *argha* vessel.

Having placed a vessel containing water, fragrance, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) while reciting the seed-syllable *hrāṃ*, and having offered a flower to each [deity] within it with the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅga*), veiled it with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), and protected it with the weapon-mantra (*astra*); then, having sprinkled oneself and the flowers and other materials with that water, one becomes empowered. Having meditated on the syllable *hrauṃ* as the red [deity] of the [Kaula] lineage, pervaded by its rays, and as oneself in the form of the Kula-Sun to be described hereafter, one should perform the ritual placement of hands (*karanyāsa*) and so forth.
Namely:
5 HRĀṂ 5 on the two little fingers; 5 HRĪṂ [— — — —] 5 HRŪṂ 5 on the two middle fingers; HRAIṂ on the two index fingers; 5 HRAUṂ 5 on the two thumbs;
(5 HRAḤ 5) on the palms and backs of the hands.

(10a) Having thus placed [the mantras] upon the heart, head, crest, armor, eyes, and the ten directions, one should then perform [the visualization]: having fashioned [the deity] as white, with a single face, seated upon a lotus, wearing a crown, earrings, the Kaustubha gem, and a forest garland, clad in yellow garments, endowed with seven hoods, with a red lotus at the navel, two-armed, holding a discus in the right hand and a conch in the left— having meditated in this manner.

Having worshipped with "Aṃ, five times; Aṃ, for Anantāsana, Aṃ, five times," one should meditate on the syllable *Hrauṃ* in the pericarp of a red six-petalled lotus at the Svādhiṣṭhāna through the practice of *kumbhaka*.

Then, by means of the wind-contraction carrying a red drop from its crest, one causes it to descend into the navel-lotus of Ananta. From that, [one visualizes] the red [deity], three-eyed, with matted hair and a yellowish-brown top-knot, having the appearance of a sixteen-year-old, four-armed, and holding [objects] in the right [hands].

Having meditated [on the deity] holding a trident and the gesture of granting boons in his left hands, holding a lotus and a bell, with fangs bared in a terrifying mien, wearing a garland of severed heads, clad in a tiger skin, with a lion skin as an upper garment, and adorned with serpents, bones, jewels, and gold—one should offer the *argha* once, saying: "O Kulamārtaṇḍa, *rahara-kṣrū-aṃ*, *rahara-kṣrū-aṃ*, I offer *argha*," and then worship him thrice and satisfy him thrice. Then, with the mantra "Hrāṃ, O Kulamārtaṇḍa, to the heart, Hrāṃ," one should worship the head, the crest-lock (*śikhā*), the armor (*kavaca*), the eyes, and the weapons upon the deity in that order. Thereafter:

"Hrāṃ 5! O Blessed One, I worship the Bhogās of Kulamārtaṇḍa, hrāṃ 5. Having thus requested the command, one draws [the deity] from the heart of the Bindu-deity in the form of a throbbing red star, places him upon the leaf of fire, and meditates on the deity arising therefrom—red, two-armed, holding a lotus and displaying the boon-granting gesture (*varada*), seated in the *padmāsana* posture, and adorned with ornaments like a god—and [establishes him] within the heart as before.

Thus, on the hare-leaf [diagram], one should worship with the *netra* [mantra] a white [deity] in the northwest holding a head, a black one in the southeast for the *śikhā*, a yellow one in the northwest for the *kavaca*, and one of lightning-color in front of the deity holding a boon-granting bell; likewise, in the east, a pale-white one holding a trident and a lotus. Similarly, in the south, a black one; in the west, a dark-blue one; and in the north, a pale-yellow one—this is the fourfold array of weapons (*astra*). Having worshipped them with the *astra* [mantra], thereafter...

*Hrāṃ*, five times, for the Eye of Kulamārtaṇḍa; *hrāṃ*, five times. Or [one may offer] with the root mantra (*mūla*). Having thus offered perfume, flowers, and so forth, and having bound the Yoni-mudrā as before, one should likewise offer the *arghya* with the root mantra, including the limbs (*aṅga*s). Then, having again offered a flower to the deity with the root mantra, one should instantly dissolve the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*) into the heart of the deity. Having led the deity, who is in the form of a drop (*bindu*), into the abode of the heart-drop, one should smell the *nirmālya* (the remains of the offering) with the heart mantra and discard it. This is the offering of the *arghya* to Kulamārtaṇḍa. 0.

Then, having sipped water and sprinkled mantra-water upon his head, he should turn facing west; sitting with his knees together, he should fashion a square mandala with pure cow dung using the *praṇavas* according to the requirements of the worship. Therein, having drawn a square in accordance with the arrival [of the deities] by reciting "Aiṃ 5 maṃtra-maṇḍalāya aiṃ 5," [he should place it] in its northeast corner.

Having placed [the thumb] upon the right big toe, one should visualize again above it the earth element, yellow, square, marked with a vajra; the water element, in the form of a liquid, dark-blue and white, marked with white water-lilies and blue lotuses;

the fire element, triangular, red, marked with a svastika; the wind element, six-cornered, smoke-colored, marked with six dots; and the space element, circular, white, marked with the sound [syllable].

Having written the syllables *laṃ*, *vaṃ*, *raṃ*, *yaṃ*, *haṃ*, *saṃ*— which have the form of a *nāda* and are intensely red— enclosed within the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) for each individual letter, arranged according to the sequence of entry into the six maṇḍalas; and having encircled them three times with *praṇavas* in the manner of the flowing wind.

Having worshipped them once more with those same [mantras], one should create a circular mandala on the square panel by moving in the direction of the wind (counter-clockwise) using either the ring finger or the thumb, starting from the east with "5 kā 5".

One should worship it with: "5 kā kāmamaṇḍalāya kā 5". In this manner, having created the mandalas in sequence with their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*), one should worship them with their respective seed-syllables as follows:
*khā* Khecarī; *gā* Guru; *ghā* Ghanojvala; *ṅā* Rudra; *cā* Candra in the northeast corner; *chā* Chāyā in the south; *jā* Jaya; *jhā* Jhākāra; *ñā* Jñāna; *ṭā* Some.
(13a) *Ṭhā* Lāṅgalī; *Ḍā* Ḍāmara in the southwest (*nairṛtya*); *Ḍhā* Ardhanārīśvara in the west (*paścima*); *Ṇā* Umākānta; *Taṃ* Āṣāḍhī; *Thā* Ḍiṇḍī; *Dā* Dhātrīśa; *Dhā* Mīna;
*Nā* Meṣa in the northwest (*vāyu*); *Pā* Lohita; *Phā* Śikhin in the north (*uttara*); *Bā* Khaḍgīśa; *Bhā* Dvi(ra)ṇḍa; *Mā* Kāla; *Yā* Vālin; *Rā* Bhuṅga in the northeast (*īśa*).

*Lā pinākī*. One who is unable to worship each of these individually should perform the worship in the center with this mantra: *Ā* (five times), from the twenty-eight *krama*-maṇḍalas, *Aṃ* (five times).

Thereafter, having raised the thumb, [in the] center: *5 Hsraṃ Mahāvahnipretāsanāya Hsraṃ* (five times). *5 Aiṃ Praṇavamaṇḍalavyāpi-pādāya Vicce Aiṃ* (five times). Having worshipped thus, one should place the Āgama upon it. This is the Āgama-maṇḍala.

(13b) Then, at the beginning of the [next] transmission (*āgama*), having released the three thumbs, by means of the upward-moving wind through the yoga of the five *praṇavas*, there is a red [wind] of twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in the right wind by way of a clockwise rotation;

a white [wind] of sixteen finger-breadths in the left wind by way of a counter-clockwise rotation; and a [wind] of twenty-four finger-breadths in the middle wind by means of both hands joined together and rotated upward to the left and right.

Having fashioned a square mandala that is intensely red, one should leave aside one finger’s breadth in its center and complete a circle through the application of breath-retention (*kumbhaka*). Placing the right thumb in the northeast corner (*īśāna-koṇa*), one should fashion three circles above the [initial] circle by means of a clockwise rotation, using the ring fingers together with flowers, each separated by the space of one finger, following the path of entry. In their center...

Having drawn an eight-petalled lotus and having applied the flower to the pericarp with the five *praṇavas*, one should then meditate upon the first circle as white, marked by a half-moon and the *hrīḥ* syllable. [OṂ] *vāṃ* [OṂ] *candramaṇḍalāya* [OṂ] *vāṃ* [OṂ]. Having thus worshipped it, one should likewise meditate upon the second circle as red, marked by a dot (*bindu*). [RĀ] *rāṃ* [RĀ] *sūryamaṇḍalāya* [RĀ] *rāṃ* [RĀ]. The third circle is intensely red, marked by a line (*nāda*). [KṢĀ] *kṣāṃ* [KṢĀ] *vahnimaṇḍalāya* [KṢĀ] *kṣāṃ* [KṢĀ]. Arising from the *nāda*, it is red; the yellow [circle] is the *maṇḍaka*.

Having meditated upon a dark seed-syllable (*bīja*) within a lotus that has white, red, and yellow filaments, one should worship with "Śrīṃ raktapadmāya Śrīṃ" five times. Following that, having worshipped the twenty-eight previously mentioned maṇḍalas in the center of the square and the circle according to the previously stated sequence, one should worship once in the center using the previously mentioned mantra for the powerless (*aśakti*).

Thereafter, having worshipped Vahni Svāhā with the mantra to be recited for the lotus-feet: *Aiṃ Akhaṇḍamaṇḍalavyāpi Pādāya Vicce Aiṃ* (five times), one should offer flowers three times with the root mantra, saying: *Iyattvā Kevalaṃ Deva*. Thus ends the Guru-maṇḍala.

Thereafter: having left three finger-breadths in front of that [central point] and prepared a vessel-maṇḍala measuring five finger-breadths with five *praṇavas*, [one offers] "5 aiṃ to the vessel-maṇḍala, aiṃ 5," and places a flower upon it. Thereafter: having offered flowers in the east, south, west, north, and center with the five-jewel mantra (*pañcaratnamantra*) to be described, the vessel-maṇḍala is completed. Then, having drawn a staff-shaped maṇḍala to the right of the deity-maṇḍala, [one recites] "5 aiṃ to the door-guardian maṇḍala, aiṃ 5. Thus, having worshipped the door-guardian maṇḍala in its three parts.
To the left of the deity, there is a square [mandala] with a circle in the center marked by five lotuses. [Reciting] "AṂ Kula-caṇḍa-caṇḍāya AṂ" five times, one should worship this Caṇḍa-maṇḍala.

In this manner, the four maṇḍalas should be prepared according to the Samādhi[-tantra], even in the absence of all [materials]. Alternatively, having washed one's hands with cow dung, or in the absence of a cloth made of silk, gold, or other such materials—
Having placed a cloth consecrated with the *astra-mantra* upon it, one should worship the deity; such is the arrangement of the five mandalas.

Then, having assumed the *svastika* posture, one should prepare a vessel upon the mandala, filled with water consisting of three parts—excellent flowers and fragrance—and washed with the *praṇavas* of Viśvāmitra and the other [mantras]. [The syllables] *pā pū* arise from the heart, the left arm, and the throat, on the right petal. Yoga is black, holding a sword and a threatening gesture in his hands. Kaumārī is red, with a spear and the gesture of granting boons in her hands, adorned with three crests and a diadem.

Having meditated upon Yamāsanā, who is dark blue, and [upon] Astrāsanā as before— [in the great field of] Kollāpura, Cā, Chā, Jā, Jhā, Ñā, Yogamahābhairava, Kaumārī, Ū, Ū̃, Ūhāyī, Parā, Avvā, Pā, Pū. (31b)

[One should meditate upon] Harasiddha, who arises from the heart, navel, right side, and throat; he is blue, located on the southwest petal, and holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. [One should meditate upon] Vaiṣṇavī, who is dark green, holds a discus and the gesture of granting boons, is adorned with crocodile earrings and a crown, and is seated upon the southwest. Having meditated upon Ṛṣā, who is blue-colored and seated upon a corpse, [one recites]: "In the great field of Aṭṭahāsa:
Ṭaṃ Ṭhaṃ Ḍaṃ Ḍhaṃ Ṇaṃ, O Harasiddha Mahābhairava, Vaiṣṇavī, Ṛṃ Ṛṃ Ṛṣāyī, Parā Avvā, Pā Pū. [One should meditate upon her] arising from the navel, left side, and throat.

(32a) On the western petal: having meditated upon Bhaṭṭa, who is pale-white and holds a sword and a blue lotus; and Vārāhī, who is blue-red, holding a mace and displaying the gesture of granting boons, with the face of a sow, her hair tawny and tied upward in a bun, seated upon a corpse;
and likewise [the goddess] Ḷṣā, who is pale-white in color, seated upon a weapon as before; [and the seed-syllables] Taṃ Thaṃ Daṃ Dhaṃ Naṃ in the great field of Jayantāpura.

Bhaṭṭamahābhairava, Vārāhī, ḶṂ ḶṂ ḶṢĀYĪ, Parā, Avvā, PĀ PŪ. [The syllables] arising from the navel, the liṅga, the right and left sides of the abdomen, the back, the navel, the heart, and the throat. On the wind-petal: KILAKILAṂ, greenish-black like a mung-bean, holding a sword and a severed head; Indrāṇī, yellow, holding a vajra and displaying the boon-granting gesture, with a thousand eyes, adorned with a crown of five tufts of hair.

Having meditated upon the seat of Vāyu as red and the seat of Astra as before, [one should worship] in the great field of Caritra: *pā phā bā bhā mā kila kila mahābhairavendrāṇī eṃ aiṃ aiṣāyī parā avvā pā pū*. From the linga, anus, and head down to the feet, [is] that which originates from the throat. On the northern petal is Kālarātri, fair-complexioned, holding a broom and a threatening gesture; Cāmuṇḍā is red, possessing skin and bone, with the rest [of her attributes]; she has matted hair of tawny hue with a crescent moon, holds a sword and a threatening gesture, and sits upon the seat of Kubera—*auvāyī*.

Having meditated upon Gaurī, who is white in complexion and seated upon a bull, [one should contemplate] her who resides in the great field of Ekāmra—she who is Rā, Lā, Vā, Kālarātri, Mahābhairavī, Cāmuṇḍā, Oṃ, Auṃ, Auṃvāyī, Parā, Avvā, Pā, Pū. From the anus, the bow, the feet, up to the head, she arises from the rays of the throat. On the eastern petal is the terrifying, white Mahālakṣmī, holding a skull and a ḍiṇḍima drum.

Having meditated upon her as golden-hued, adorned with a crown of matted locks and a tiara, holding a lotus and the gesture of granting boons, seated upon Īśāna, white in color, and with weapons and seats as previously described—one should contemplate [the syllables] *śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ kṣaṃ* at the great field of Devīkoṭa for Bhīṣaṇamahābhairava; and *ma(hāṃ) lakṣmī aṃ aḥ aḥ hlāyī parā avvā pā pū*.
These should be understood as Maṅgalabrahmāṇī, whose names are thus declared, possessing identical forms, weapons, and seats.

(33b) According to another alternative, one should worship these [deities] starting from Jayantī and ending with Aṭṭahāsa, and from the West ending with Nairṛtya. Following that, having worshipped and satisfied the two deities in three ways according to the tradition, and having worshipped the limbs of dissolution (*layāṅga*), one should worship the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*) preceded by a request for permission (*ājñāprārthanā*). Thus: *Aiṃ Bhagavan*...

"I worship the nine [deities] who are my own self and the limbs of enjoyment, Aiṃ 5. Having thus requested permission from the Lord, one should [visualize him] on the tip of a flame-petal or within a solar mandala—

white, four-faced, four-armed, seated in the lotus posture upon a white lotus, in the *tribhaṅga* pose, with curly hair that is tawny at the top, wearing a crescent moon and a garland of severed heads.

Having meditated [on the deity] wearing a tiger skin, with a divine cloth as an upper garment, holding the boon-granting gesture (*varada-mudrā*) and a spear (*śakti*) in the right hand, and holding a trident (*śūla*) and a rosary (*japya*) in the left; [recite]: *ha sa* five times for the Heart of Navātman, *ha sa* five times, *pā pū*, in the northeast (*īśe*). Likewise, [meditate on] the fair-complexioned one arisen from the *uṣṇīṣa*, with a form as before, [holding] a weapon and striking the earth—[recite]: *kṣa ma* five times for the Head of Navātman, *pā pū*, in the southwest (*naiṛtye*). [Meditate on] the red one arisen from the *śikhā*, with a form as before—[recite]: *la* five times for the Tuft (*śikhā*), *la va* five times, *pā pū*.

From the head, the [mantra] arising from the rays reaching to the feet is *vāyau* (*vāyave*), black, as before, [placed] in the heart: *ya ra 5*, for the armor consisting of nine parts: *ya ra 5*. *pā pū*.

(34b) Arising from the rays of the three eyes, [it is placed] in the pericarp. On the right side of the deity—in front—at the neck: extremely red, as before: *5 ū*, for the three eyes consisting of nine parts.

*Ūṃ 5 Pā Pū*. Having meditated upon [the deity] born from the rays of the trident in the east, born from the rays in the south, born from the rays of the banner in the west, and born from the rays of the remaining arms in the north—[a form that is] tawny, with a face terrifying with fangs, and a lolling tongue, endowed with weapons and a threatening gesture as before—one should worship the four weapons starting from the east with: *Aṃ Navātma-astrāya Aṃ 5 Pā Pū*. Then, having requested permission, one worships the limbs of enjoyment for the Goddess Samayā with: *Aiṃ Bhagavati Samayāyai bhogāṅgān pūjayāmi Aiṃ 5*. *Ājñāṃ prārthya*. (Having requested permission.)

(35a) The goddess arises from the light-rays of the heart; she is the limb of the deity within the lunar mandala of speech. Having meditated upon the goddess as being like the heart of the deity, [one recites]: *Hsphrāṃ namo bhagavati kamalāyi hsphrāṃ samayā hṛdayāya* five times, *pā pū*. Thus, having worshipped up to the eyes with the mantras of the goddess's limbs, one [worships] that which arises from the twelve arms.

And one should likewise worship the *astra*. Again, when there is the authority [to do so], [one should recite]: *5 hrāṃ navātmahṛdayāya 5 pā pū*. Having thus formed the *kūṭa* (syllabic cluster) modified by the six vowels, one should perform the worship of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) of the deity alone; this is the worship of the limbs for enjoyment (*bhogāṅgapūjā*).
Thereafter, having worshipped the two deities in three ways: *5 ha sa navātmane gandhaṃ ha sa 5*, or with the root mantra (*mūla*): *5 hsphrāṃ namo bhagavati kamalāyi*.

(35b) Hsphrāṃ, perfume 5. Or with the root mantra: 5 Aiṃ, Maṅgala-Mahābhairava-Brahmāṇau, aiṃ, perfume 5. Aiṃ, perfume for Ākhyā, aiṃ 5. In this same manner, it should be understood for the other groups of eight. 5 Ha Sa, perfume for Navātmahṛdaya, ha sa 5. Hsphrāṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Lady Kamalā, hsphrāṃ.

5 *samayā* for the heart, [offering] fragrance; likewise for the others as well. Thereafter, having offered flowers, incense, lamps, water for sipping (*ācamana*), food offerings (*naivedya*), water for sipping, betel leaves, and so forth to all with this very mantra, and having performed the satiation (*tarpaṇa*) of all with their respective root mantras beginning with fragrance and the rest, the food offering should be given with the word *svāhā* at the end. Then, sounding the bell according to the sequence to be described, one offers incense and lamps. Then...

(36a) Having first satisfied all [the deities] beginning with the gods, and having again worshipped the two deities in three ways, one should offer *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) while reciting the heart-mantra. Then, having displayed the five mudrās— the *yoni*, *śaṅkha*, *padma*, *triśikhā*, and *añjali*— beginning with the *vāgbhava* syllable, one should take up the well-established rosary with the syllable *aiṃ*, sprinkle it with *hrīṃ*, and [arrange it] in the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*) with *śrīṃ*.

Having worshipped with sandalwood water, having fumigated with *hsphreṃ*, and having offered flowers with *hsauṃ*, one should worship the two deities with their respective mantras and perform recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity. Then, one should offer it as follows:
*5 hrūṃ srūṃ 5 navātmānandanātha-samayāparā avvāyai japaṃ gṛhāṇa*. In the case of separate recitations for each, [the mantra is]: *5 hrūṃ 5*.
(36b) "O Lord, accept the recitation for Navātmanandanātha; having offered it into the hand of the Bestower of Boons—*srūṃ* five times. O Blessed One, accept the recitation for Samayā;

having offered it into the left hand. Having performed the recitation for the limbs (*aṅga*) at one-tenth the amount [of the main mantra] and offered it, one should place the heart-garland (*hṛdāmālā*) in its own place. In the case of finger-recitation (*karajāpya*), one should purify the hand with *praṇavas*."

Holding flowers, *dūrvā* grass, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) in his hands, he should perform the recitation (*jāpya*). If he has the capacity, he should sprinkle the incense vessel with water while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*, take up the bell with the *vāgbhava-mantra*, and taking hold of both the incense vessel and the bell with the *netra-mantra*, ring the bell and fumigate the two deities with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*). Having sprinkled the lamp vessel with the *astra-mantra* and ignited it with the *śikhā-mantra*, he should offer wicks of seasonal oil with the root mantra and rotate [the lamp] five times in the manner of the wind's movement.

(37a) Again, having worshipped the two deities three times and having fallen with knees and elbows upon the ground, [one should worship] with the *natimudrā* while holding flowers to the heart: "Victory to you, O Lord of the Three Worlds, the ninefold self, the supreme self! Victory to you, the omnipresent one; salutations to you who are established upon the crown of the head! Mounted upon the seat of the syllable *Aiṃ*, seated above the vajra-lotus, you have entered the six aspects."
I bow to the Goddess Śrī Kubjikā. Having praised her with other hymns of Śambhu or with hymns to the Divine Couple, one should cast a handful of flowers at their feet and perform prostration;
this is the worship of the Guru-maṇḍala.

Now, having sprinkled the head three times with the water of the *argha* offering, and having formed a yellow square by revolving the five *praṇavas* over the heart, one should form a yellow square to its west.

(37b) 5 *Lamayrūṃ* 5. Having emanated by means of this [seed-syllable] and having worshipped it once with this very same [mantra], [one draws] a dark-blue half-moon in the north. 5 *Vamayrūṃ* 5. Likewise, having emanated and worshipped it, [one draws] a red triangle in the south. 5 *Ramayrūṃ* 5. Likewise, having emanated and worshipped it, [one draws] a smoke-colored hexagon in the east. 5 *Yamayrūṃ* 5. Likewise, having emanated and worshipped it...

Above that is a red circular mandala: *ramayrūṃ* five times, for the sake of liberation from passion; having emanated it with this [mantra] and worshipped it with this very [mantra], above that is a smoke-colored red: *damayrūṃ* five times, for the sake of liberation from hatred; having emanated it and worshipped it with this [mantra], above that is a reddish-brown: *mamayrūṃ*, for the sake of liberation from delusion.

In the same manner, having fashioned [the lotus] and worshipped it, upon that [is drawn] a red-colored eight-petaled lotus with filaments, a pericarp, and nine seed-syllables: *Śrīṃ Rāṃ* for the great red lotus, *Rāṃ Śrīṃ*.

In the same manner, having fashioned and worshipped it, [one places] a white circle upon the pericarp: *Hlāṃ* for the maṇḍala of beings, *Hlāṃ*. In the same manner, having fashioned and worshipped it...

Above that, having likewise fashioned and worshipped the red *rūṃ* five times for the *rajas-maṇḍala*, and above that, having likewise fashioned and worshipped the fire-colored *kṣūṃ* five times for the *tamas-maṇḍala*; and above that, having likewise fashioned and worshipped the white, crystal-like sphere (*golaka*) five times with *hamayrūṃ* five times; and above that, having likewise fashioned and worshipped the six-cornered, red-colored interior of Vāgbhava five times with *glūṃ slūṃ mlūṃ plūṃ nlūṃ laṃ vaṃ raṃ yaṃ haṃ saṃ* five times; thereafter, with the syllable *aiṃ*.

From the foundation—the navel, the *liṅga*, the heart, the throat, and the bow—one should emit a mass of rays above the six-spoked [wheel] and envelop it with the *mātṛkā* [alphabet]. Having produced the twenty-eight-fold sequence arising from that, whose nature will be described later, one should worship it as follows, on the western peak: a group of four, yellow, short, pot-bellied, with bodies sixteen years of age, and with curly, upward-pointing, tawny hair.

[One should meditate on] the Lord with a crescent moon upon his head, terrifying with his fangs, with a smiling face, two-armed, holding a breast and a water-pot in his hands, intent on gazing at the face of the Goddess Īśvarī, wearing a garland of severed heads, clothed in a tiger skin, with a divine garment as an upper robe, adorned with various flower garlands,

seated in the half-lotus posture upon a red lotus from the navel of Brahmā, embraced by the Goddess; and likewise the Goddess, who with her embracing hand holds a cluster of *pāriyātra* flowers, who with her left hand holds a skull-cup filled with all nectars, who likewise gazes at the Lord, and who sits upon a royal throne as the Mother of the Samaya.
Having meditated, one should worship the fourfold seat with: *brāṃ* for the seat of Brahmā-Pretāsana, *braṃ* 5, and so forth.
(39b) *lamayrūṃ oḍiyāṇamahāpīṭha oḍeśvarānandanātha oḍeśvarīparā avvā lamayrūṃ 5 pā pū*.
5 *Vam-ay-rūṃ*. Jālandhara Mahāpīṭha, Jāleśvara Ānandanātha, Jāleśvarī Parā Avvā, *vam-ay-rūṃ* 5.
*Pā Pū*. 5 *Ram-ay-rūṃ*. Pūrṇagiri Mahāpīṭha, Pūrṇeśvara Ānandanātha, Pūrṇeśvarī Parā Avvā, *ram-ay-rūṃ* 5.
*Pā Pū*. 5 *Yam-ay-rūṃ*. Kāmarūpa Mahāpīṭha, Kāmeśvara Ānandanātha, Kāmeśvarī Parā Avvā, *yam-ay-rūṃ* 5. *Pā Pū*.
Thus is the group of four seats (*pīṭha*).
On the peak of the wind is the group of five. Likewise, [there is] the dark one seated upon Viṣṇu-Preta. *Vīṃ* to Viṣṇu-Pretāsana, *vīṃ*.
Having worshipped the group of five: *glūṃ* Śrīkaṇṭhānandanātha, Gaganāparā, Avvā, *glūṃ*, *pā*, *pū*. [5] *slūṃ* Anantānandanātha, Svargāparā, Avvā, *slūṃ*, [5] *pā*, *pū*.
5 mlūṃ Śaṃkarānandanātha, the mortal Aparā Avvā, mlūṃ 5 pā pū.
5 plūṃ Piṅgalānandanātha, the Pātālā Aparā Avvā, plūṃ 5 pā pū. 5 nlūṃ Sādākhyānandanātha, the Nāgā Aparā Avvā, nlūṃ 5 pā pū.
Thus is the pentad. On the peak of Īśāna is the seat of Rudra, likewise fivefold and red:
*RŪ* five times for the Rudra-preta-seat, *RŪ* five times.
Having worshipped six times:
5 Ḍamayrū̃ Ānandanātha-Ḍākinī Parā Avvā Ḍamayrū̃ 5 Pā Pū (40b).

5 Ramayrūṃ, Āvalyānandanātha, Rākinī, Parā, Avvā, Ramayrūṃ, 5 Pā Pū. 5 Lamayrūṃ, Predvānandanātha, Lākinī, Parā, Avvā, Lamayrūṃ, 5 Pā Pū. 5 Kamayrūṃ, Yogyānandanātha, Kākinī, Parā, Avvā, Kamayrūṃ, 5 Pā Pū.
5 *samayrūṃ*, [to] Ānandanātha, Sākinī, Parā, Avvā, *samayrūṃ* 5, *pā pū*.
5 *hamayrūṃ*, [to] Pādānandanātha, Hākinī, Parā, Avvā, *hamayrūṃ* 5, *pā pū*.
Thus is the group of six Nāthas.
On the eastern peak, a smoke-colored square. 5 Ī Īśvarapretāsanāya Ī 5. Worship in four ways (41a).
5 *laṃ* Ādhārīśānandanātha, Raktā Parā Avvā, *lāṃ* 5 *pā pū*.
5 *vāṃ* Cakrīśānandanātha, Caṇḍā Parā Avvā, *vāṃ* 5 *pā pū*.
5 *rāṃ* Kuraṅgīśānandanātha, Karālā Avvā, *rāṃ* 5 *pā pū*.

Yaṃ Madandhrīśānandanātha Mahocchuṣmā Parā Avvā Yā Pā Pū. Thus is the tetrad of the Lords of the Ages (yugeśa). On the peak of Agni is the white seat of Sadāśiva. 5 Saṃ [to] Sadāśiva on the corpse-seat, saṃ 5. Having worshipped in five ways:
5 GĀ Anādivimalānandanātha, Mātaṅgīparā Avvā GĀ 5 PĀ PŪ | 5 SĀ Sarvajñavimalānandanātha, Pulindinīparā Avvā SAṂ 5 PĀ PŪ | (41b)
5 maṃ [to] Yogavimalānandanātha Śavarī Parā Avvā mā 5 pā pū | 5 pā [to] Siddhavimalānandanātha Campā Parā Avvā pā 5 pā pū | 5 nā [to] Samayavimalānandanātha Samayā Parā Avvā naṃ 5 pā pū |

Thus ends the Vimalapañcaka. On the southwestern peak: a deep red lotus seat or a corpse seat of Śiva. RĀ RĀ RĀ RĀ RĀ: *Oṃ rā rā rā rā rā*, to the corpse seat of the red lotus, *rā*. ŚĪ ŚĪ ŚĪ ŚĪ ŚĪ: *Oṃ śī śī śī śī śī*, to the corpse seat of Śiva, *śī*.
Or thus:
having worshipped in four ways— lamayrūṃ, Mitrānandanātha Kuleśvarī Parā Avvā lamayrūṃ 5, pā pū.
5 VAMAYRŪṂ, OḌĀNANDANĀTHA, LAGHVĪPARĀ AVVĀ, VAMAYRŪṂ 5 PĀ PŪ.
(42a) 5 RAMAYRŪṂ, ṢAṢṬHĀNANDANĀTHA, KUBJIKĀPARĀ AVVĀ, RAMAYRŪṂ 5 PĀ PŪ.
*Yamayūrū Carya-Nandanātha-Kuja-Aparā Avvā Yamayūrū 5 Pā Pū*.
Thus is the mouth of the Guru.

These [deities] should be understood as being equal to the first tetrad and having the form of seats (*āsana*). Together with the Goddess, one should again worship the divine seat (*devāsana*) in the center, just as before.
Above that, one should meditate upon the Supreme Lord, whose form is as previously described, seated upon a throne consisting of half [of his consort].
One should visualize the Goddess also in the previously described form, seated upon the lap of the Lord with her pair of feet placed upon the navel-lotus, and worship her as follows:
*hrūṃ srūṃ au o srūṃ hrūṃ*—Navātmānandanātha, Samayā, Aparā, Avvā; *pā pū*.

Having worshipped [them] three times and gratified [them] three times with this, thereafter, one should gratify each of the deities of the lineage (*kramadevatā*) individually with their respective mantra: *hrūṃ srūṃ*, [offering to] Navātmānandanātha, Samayāparā, and Avvā. Having given these perfumes (*gandha*) and so forth, as before, one should gratify them in three ways.
5. Oṃ, twenty-eight times to the gods; this is the limb [of the ritual]. Having thus offered flowers and the other articles, [one recites]:
"I bow to the venerable Kubjikā, the goddess born from the secret wheel (guhyacakra), who resides upon the sacred seats and fields (kṣetrapīṭha), and who bestows the three commands (ājñā)."
I bow to that Goddess Kubjikā, the source of the universe of moving and unmoving beings,
who stands as the singular embodiment of coming and going;
she is the power of churning Bhairava and is the very nature of the foundational seat (adhiṣṭhāna).
(43a) I bow to the goddess Śrī Kubjikā, who possesses infinite attributes;
as Mālinī in the form of the Bindu, she fills all that is moving and unmoving.
I bow to Śrī Kubjikā, who consists of the essence of the five elements.
I bow to Śrī Kubjikā, who resides on the wheel of the potter’s lathe, producing the great sound within the Unstruck (anāhata) that pervades the sphere from Śiva down to the earth.
I bow to the goddess Śrī Kubjikā, the Great Māyā of the subtle body, who abides in the state that is both supreme and non-supreme, and who dwells in the condition of fullness.
She is Agriṇī, Mālinī, Sarvā, Jyeṣṭhā, and likewise Anāmikā.
I bow to Raudrī, Manonmanī, and Śrī Kubjikā;
she has transcended all states of being, is beyond comparison, and abides in the state of the mindless.
I bow to the goddess Śrī Kubjikā, whose bones are full;
who is accompanied by the Siddhacakra, who resides within the four seats (pīṭhas),
and who is independent and liberated by her own command— I bow to Śrī Kubjikā.
I bow to the goddess Śrī Kubjikā, who has entered the path of the Kula, who is established in various locations, and who is the goddess whose command is intensely powerful.
She has come down through the lineage of succession and was spoken by the Peak of the Command (Ājñāśikhara).

I bow to the lineage of the Siddhas and to the stainless Supreme Goddess. In the triangle (*śṛṅgāṭa*) maṇḍala at the summit of that which is known as Sadāmṛta, and in the great wheel (*mahācakra*) of Koṅkaṇa, I bow to the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśī*) according to the tradition (*samaya*).
Having thus praised and again satisfied the two deities with the *yonimudrā*, one should bind the Goddess with *pūraka* [breath-retention], following the sequence with the heart-mantra and the mind.

Having dissolved the two deities into one another and having caused them to dissolve into the *vāgbhava* syllable, one should draw the flower from the head [of the deity] into the joined palms, smell it with the *devahṛdaya* mantra, and slowly place it in the northern part of the circle of Caṇḍa.
This is the superior method (*uttama-pakṣa*). As for the middling method (*madhyama-pakṣa*), one should likewise sprinkle the head with *praṇavas* and fashion a hexagon.
5 ĀṂ! From the twenty-eight seats of the Krama, ĀṂ!

5. Having worshipped the seat in the center with this single sentence alone, one should emanate a mass of rays from the *brahmarandhra* by means of the syllable AIṂ; having meditated upon the host of Krama deities produced therefrom—(44b)

Having worshipped according to the stated sequence and having likewise sacrificed to the two deities in due order, one should lead [the deity] into dissolution in the *brahmarandhra*. In the lower alternative (*adhamapakṣa*): having likewise performed the sprinkling of the head and fashioned a hexagon, [one offers] "Oṃ, oṃ, to the seat of the twenty-eight-fold sequence, oṃ."
Having worshipped the seat in the center with this [mantra], and having meditated upon those two who have arisen from the mass of rays in the *brahmarandhra*—
namely, 5 *hrūṃ srūṃ*, Aṣṭāviṃśatnavātmānandanātha, and Aṣṭāviṃśatnavātmikā Aparā Avvā, *srūṃ hrūṃ* 5 *pā pū*—
one should worship and satisfy them three times with this.

Again, having worshipped them in the same manner with the *saṃpuṭa* mantra, one should effect their dissolution (*laya*) right there in the *brahmarandhra*. In the system of sequential worship (*kramārccana*), the worship of the seat (*āsanapūjā*) is performed on the head;
however, this sequential worship may also be performed without it, by placing [the hands] at the feet or by wrapping [them] around the head. This is the *Śrīkramārccana*.
Then, having worshipped the two deities in three ways and having fallen with knees and elbows upon the ground:
"OṂ ĀṂ BHAGAVAN NAVĀTMAN BHAGAVATI SAMAYĀYE VAHNĀU CARCCAYIṢYĀMI ĀṂ 5.

Having thus obtained permission and taken the *argha* water with the six seed-syllables, [he prepares a pit] eighteen finger-breadths deep, twenty-two finger-breadths wide, with a neck one finger-breadth thick and six finger-breadths high.

There is one broad girdle (*mekhalā*). Above that is the *yoni*, which is slightly curved inward like an *aśvattha* leaf, eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) wide, twelve finger-breadths long, and one finger-breadth high. Below this is a lotus with petals one finger-breadth wide, a stalk seven finger-breadths long, and a base three finger-breadths wide, upon which rests a somewhat beautiful wheel attached to the ground.

The bulbous root [of the sacrificial pit] should be four finger-breadths wide, and its shape should be either square, triangular, or hexagonal. Having thus constructed the *bhūta-kuṇḍa*, one should gaze upon it with the eyes, sprinkle it with water using the *astra-mantra*, smear it with clay using the *kāca-mantra*, and fashion a lotus in the center using the *vāgbhava-mantra*. Thereafter, having sprinkled the blazing fire with the *astra-mantra*, one should project it into the center of the pit using the seed-syllable *yūṃ*—the *tejīśa-kūṭa*—accompanied by the *khaṭaka* gesture. Then, by means of inhalation (*pūraka*), the heart-mantra of the deity, and the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, one should draw that consciousness, resembling the flame of a lamp, from the fire into the *bindu*.

Having established the seed-syllable *raṃ* right there and visualized it in its blazing form, one should unify oneself with it; then, having contemplated the syllable *kṣā* at the navel as endowed with seven rays,

and having merged it into the state of the drop (*bindu*) by entering through the *suṣumnā* channel, one should draw forth that energy— which resembles the flame of a burning lamp— by means of the *udbhava-mudrā* and the peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) of *Tejīśa*.

Having placed that fire and the oblation materials into the fire situated in the *kuṇḍa*, one should gaze upon them thrice with the ninefold self (*navātman*). Then, having meditated upon [the deity] as being within the splendor of the *tejīsa* syllables, seated upon a red lotus on a red lotus, squatting with a protruding belly, with tawny beard and matted hair standing erect, terrifying with his fangs, three-eyed, wearing red garments and an upper cloth, two-armed, granting boons, and holding a spear; |||
(46b) 5 *Khrūṃ* to Tejīśānandanātha, *khrūṃ* svāhā!

Having offered five oblations of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) with this [mantra], one should worship the two deities three times with their root mantra while in a state of non-conceptualization (*niḥsaṃjñā*). Then, having meditated upon the fire and the two deities within the heart-lotus, one should [proceed] with the mantras of the two deities according to the alternative method.

When worship has been performed by one joined with the *saṃjñā*, then, having meditated upon the two deities, one should offer sesame seeds and so forth—either smeared with ghee or smeared with the three sweets—ten parts of which have been recited (*japa*), with the mantra: *hrū̃ srū̃ navātmānandanāthāya samayāparā avvāyai svāhā*. Thereafter, having uttered the mantras of the two deities up to their dissolution (*laya*) and having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, [one should perform the concluding rites].

Having performed the offering (*samarpaṇa*) to the two deities, one should again perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) according to one's capacity with the root mantra of Tejīśa. In the case of the name-mantra of the two deities, [one offers] with the root mantra of the two deities; in the case of the heart-mantra of the deity, one should meditate on Tejīśa in the form of a *bindu* and effect its dissolution into the place of the *bindu*. Then, having prepared ash and sandalwood paste with the weapon-mantra of the deity, and having extinguished the fire with milk—or, in its absence, with pure water—one should, in the case of a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), perform the rites of inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*), smear it with cow-dung to the measure of one cubit, and following the stated sequence, [draw] a twelve-finger span [area] in the center with the syllable *aiṃ*.

(47b) Having fashioned a triangle in the shape of the syllable *aiṃ*, having placed a flower upon it with that very [syllable], and having placed a blazing fire sprinkled with the *astra-mantra* therein, one should perform the fire-sacrifice (*homakārya*) according to the stated sequence.

Now, having formed a square mandala on the right hand with the *praṇavas*, having placed a flower upon it with that very [mandala], [one should visualize] in the east [the deity] who is red, dwarfish, pot-bellied, three-eyed, and holding a *carcarī* staff aloft.

Having meditated upon [the deity] thus endowed with a specific Śakti— one adorned with a mass of matted hair and a crescent moon, wearing a garland of severed heads, two-armed, with hands in the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness, having the appearance of a sixteen-year-old, possessing a terrifying luster, seated in the lotus posture upon a white lotus on a white bull— [recite]: 5 Ā Ādigurunāthasthūlāparā Avvā Ā 5 PĀ PŪ.

(48a) Likewise, in the south, there is the yellow [syllable]. *Aṃ*, the supreme (*parā*) of the beginningless Guru—*Avvā sā pā pū*. I worship them. Having thus worshipped and satisfied them in three ways, one should lead these [deities], who are of the nature of light rays, into the fire [of the *svāhā* mantra] with the *sūkara* [pig-face] held in the hand.

(Worship of the Primordial and Subsequent Gurus) — (Now the two deities) — ... in the fierce mandala, dark as the petal of a blue lotus, in the triple-bent (tribhaṅga) posture, graceful, the three deities, with three eyes;

Or, having meditated upon [the deity] in the *vīrāsana* posture, with two arms holding a sword and a blue lotus, and possessing a body sixteen years of age;

having worshipped and gratified three times with "Śrīṃ Kulacaṇḍavāsuki Śrīṃ 5 Pā Pū," and having again worshipped the two deities once, one should bind the *yonimudrā* with the root mantra of the deity alone and contemplate the threefold worship.

Having performed the dissolution of the deities into the heart of the Lord, and having meditated upon the Lord in the form of a *bindu* in the *brahmarandhra*, likewise having led the Goddess into dissolution in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, and having joined the *āgama* mantras with the syllables of the *āgama*, one should take the *nirmālya*.
Having offered it with the mantra: "Śrīṃ Kulacaṇḍavāsuki Śrīṃ, accept this *nirmālya*," and having displayed the *phaṇāmudrā* (hood-gesture).

(49b) By raising the *tarjanī* mudrā with the palm facing upward and snapping the fingers three times while moving them upward, one effects the dissolution of Caṇḍa into space. Following that, according to the general procedure, one should worship the fourfold [set] beginning with oneself and the field (*kṣetra*). Having prepared a square mandala with the *praṇava* syllables, one places the vessel for the *bali* offering therein.

Having placed [the offering] filled with flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, and betel in the heart, or having meditated on the eight peaks (*aṣṭakūṭa*) as red and white in sequence, one should expel them by means of exhalation (*recaka*) and deposit them into that vessel. From that [vessel], the field of oneself (*ātmakṣetra*) is white, the field of the location (*sthānakṣetra*) is yellow, the island of oneself (*ātmadvīpa*) is black, and the island of the location (*sthānadvīpa*) is red; [he is] two-armed, with the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*).
Having meditated upon the gentle one with three eyes seated on a lotus throne, [one recites]:

"A Ka Ha Sa Kṣraṃ! To the Kṣetrapāla of the self, accept, accept this worship and offering; be the granter of boons to me, bring about peace, bring about peace, svāhā! Having thus offered it, [one recites]:
"Ū Jūṃ Saḥ."

Having thus satisfied [the deity] in three ways, one should lead [the consciousness] into the heart-dwelling within the heart. In the case of the *sthāna-kṣetra* [tradition], it is "to the Lord of the Place" (*sthānapataye*). In the case of the *ātma-dvīpa*, it is "to the Lord of the Island of the Self" (*ātmadvīpeśvarāya*). In the case of the *sthāna-dvīpa*, it is "to Mahocchuṣma, the Lord of the Island" (*mahocchuṣme dvīpeśvarāya*). This is to be understood as the location of the *ātma-kṣetrapāla*. This is the general worship (*sāmānyapūjā*), the worship with its specific designation (*saṃjñāpūjā*). In the practice of the island (*dvīpasādhana*), it is said: "one leads upward. (50b)

Thereafter, having worshipped the Guru three times and dissolved him according to the prescribed sequence, one should dismiss the *argha* vessel. Having sipped the *argha* water three times—preceded by the libation (*tarpaṇa*) to the virgins—and having performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*), one should withdraw with the heart-mantra all the mantras of the mandala, including the flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and garlands remaining from the worship, back into the heart.
Then, having again performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth and smeared the ground with cow dung:

"5 hrīṃ, O Acala, O Dhruva, perform [this] auspiciously, perform it, svāhā hrīṃ 5. Having thus worshipped the ground, one should recite the *Trikhaṇḍā* mantra once to remove any defects in the worship, whether by omission or excess, and then [worship] the *Samayāmbā*.

Thereafter, in the case of the *āgama* [tradition], having placed the sixfold offering (*ṣaḍargha*) before the *āgama*, one should worship it with the *praṇavas*; and having worshipped the *āgama* with the *praṇavas*, or—since the physical *āgama* may not be present—having worshipped its *liṅga*, one should perform the recollection of the desired mantra (*iṣṭāṇu*) according to one's capacity. If one has the means, one should always place that offering before the *āgama*. Since there is no physical *āgama-liṅga*, one should place that offering before oneself according to the stated sequence, likewise worship the crown of one's own head, and perform the recollection of the desired mantra. Thereafter, at this juncture, what is required...
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and other rites for the sake of accomplishment, one should offer the libation (*argha*) and perform the dismissal (*visarjana*).
Thus, in the *Paścimārcanapaddhati* by Śrī Vimalaprabodha, the daily worship (*nityārcana*), concluding with the desired recitation (*jāpya*), has been fully described.
Thus ends the first rule, concerning daily worship, in the *Paścimārcanapaddhati* composed by the venerable Ācārya Vimalaprabodha, belonging to the lineage of the Paramahaṃsa Parivrājakas.
Now, I shall describe the occasional (*naimittika*) rites, divided into nineteen types, for the attainment of the fruits of worship, according to the tradition of the *Śrīparā* and other scriptures.

In that regard, at the appropriate time, the initiated practitioner should take a new thread, have it spun, fold it ninefold, wash it with alkaline salt (*rajakṣāra*), and ensure it is free from hair, insects, and other impurities.

Having thoroughly washed the sixfold [thread] and placed it upon [the altar], one should perform the ritual bath (*snāna*) with the mantra while first receiving the command of the Guru. Having prepared the *argha* vessel like that of a deity, and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the deity preceded by meditation, one should sprinkle the thread with the *argha* water using the *astra* mantra, with curd using the *hṛdaya* mantra, and with milk using the *śiras* mantra.

Having washed [the image] with the *tanutra* [mantra], with water from the *madanahala* plant, and with pure water from the gaze; having sprinkled it again with *arghya* water while reciting the root mantra; having perfumed it; having bathed it with fragrant water; having sprinkled the two deities three times with the root mantra; having offered incense and a lamp; having displayed the *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice, and the *yonimudrā*; and having protected it with the *kavaca* [mantra], dried it, and formed it into a ball—one should perform the binding with thread as follows: for the feet, a thread sixteen or twelve finger-breadths long, with a single knot, and two such sacred threads (*pavitraka*).
By measuring the sequence of the ritual instruction, the thread-measure is one *granthi*; the purifying thread (*pavitraka*) consists of thirty-four [units]. One for the Guru; one for the disciple.
Four for the four twilight ablutions (*sandhyā-avaskanda*). Twenty-three for the thread. Eleven for the vessel of the deity. Three for the gatekeepers.

For the seat of the *āgama*, there is a triad (3). For the *āgama* itself, there is a pentad; the sixth is like the white-footed (*śuklacaraṇa*) [thread], thus making six (6) for the divine mandala. For the lotus, there is one (1). For the twenty-eight mandalas, there is a single thread with a single knot, four finger-breadths long; for the twenty-eight [mandalas], there are twenty-eight threads (28). Due to their absence, there is one sacred thread (*pavitraka*) with a single thread and a single knot, four finger-breadths long (1). For the unbroken mandala, there is one (1). For the seats of the two deities, there is a tetrad (4). For the two deities, there is one (1).

(53a) For the eight [verses] beginning with *maṅgala*, the sixteenth [unit]; for the limbs (*aṅga*), the twenty-fourth; for the four heavy syllables (*guru*), the fourth; for the row of special heavy syllables (*viśeṣaguru*), thirty;

Thus is the inference. Excluding the feet of the deity, for others, the middle-sized *pavitraka* consists of three threads, five finger-breadths [in length], and a single knot. The inferior [size] consists of one thread, five finger-breadths, and one knot. Thus is the *āsana-pavitraka* according to the non-ritual method. Thereafter, for the [main] sequence: the superior [size] is with fifty-six threads; the middle is half of that [twenty-eight]; and the inferior consists of twelve threads, three or four [finger-breadths]. The remaining [measure] is with sixteen threads. For the fourfold [division], it is four finger-breadths.

For a set of four [seats], there are four fingers [in length] with four knots. For a set of five, there are five fingers with five knots. For a set of six, there are six fingers with six knots. Thus, there are twenty-eight purifiers (*pavitraka*). (28) For a set of four seats, there are four threads, four knots, four fingers [in length], and four purifiers. For the sixfold seat (*ṣaṭkāsanam*), there are six threads, six knots, six finger-breadths, and six purifiers (6). In that case, for all the sequential seats, there are four finger-breadths [for the length], five threads for the knots, and six purifiers (6). For two [seats], there are thirty-four purifiers (34). For the two feet, there are two purifiers with knots at sixteen and twelve finger-breadths respectively (2). For the Guru, there are three (3). For the *bali* offering, there is one (1). For the four twilight rituals (*saṃdhyācatuṣkam*), there are twelve (12).

(54b) For the Sun, twenty-five (25). For Devapātra, eleven (11). For the gatekeepers, nine (9). For the seat of the Āgamas, three (3). For the Āgamas, five (5). Again, like the white foot, three purifiers (3); with two, eight (8). For the divine maṇḍala, three (3). For the twenty-eight-fold maṇḍala...

A *pavitraka* consisting of five threads, four finger-breadths in length, with four knots and twenty-eight strands; [this is one type]. In the absence [of that], a single *pavitraka* consisting of twenty-eight threads, four knots, and four finger-breadths [in length];
[this is another type]. One for the unbroken mandala; [one is] four for the two deities' seats; [and three] for the two deities.

That [total] is sixteen from the eight beginning with Namaṅgala (16). Twenty-four from the limbs (24). Four from the four Gurus (4). Thirty-three from the row of special Gurus (33). One hundred and twenty-eight from the row of general Gurus (128). Three from the Guru of the month (3). Thirty-two from the continent (32).
Twenty-eight from the place and the field (28). And three from the "ca" (3). [This is] by adding the Hetuka and others.

A thread with ten strands and ten knots, fourteen purifiers (pavitrakas), three for the front of the fire-offering (homāgra), two for oneself and one's direct guru according to the measurement of the circumference [of their bodies], and likewise for virgins and others; this constitutes the supreme [set] consisting of three hundred and sixty threads.

Excluding the two deities, the medium [sacred thread] consists of half of these [measures]; the inferior consists of half of that as well—namely, nine knots and nine finger-breadths. The very inferior consists of five threads, five finger-breadths, and five knots.

Likewise for the two attendants (carau), there are two sacred threads with ten or twelve threads, finger-breadths, and knots. For the descent of the Power (Śakti), there is one with one hundred and eight threads and fifty knots.

One *pavitraka* for each measure of worship. In the absence [of the required materials], one should omit the knots and use a thread of half that length, or half of that again; or, if nothing at all is available, it may be made even with a nine-strand thread.
For the seats of the mandala, there are five threads and five finger-breadths—(the best according to the alternative view)—[the rest follows].
(56b) Four for the four Gurus; three for the argha-vessel; one for Caṇḍa; one for each of the jars;
five for the five [vases] beginning with Vāyu; three for the islands, the self, and the fields of knowledge; and one for the self; and one for the previously mentioned sequence.

Having thus fashioned the *pavitraka* for the virgins and others from *kadamba* [wood] with the heart-mantra— [omitting the rest]— [one should do so] with saffron, red sandalwood, vermilion, lac-dye, and red ochre. Having [prepared] all [the materials], having [consecrated them] through yoga, and having [offered] praise, one should place [the *pavitrakas*] inside a new bamboo vessel with the heart-mantra, after arranging white and pure garments [around it].

Thereafter, on the eighth or fourteenth day of the month of Āṣāḍha, or likewise in Śrāvaṇa or Bhādrapada; or specifically on the fourth day of the bright fortnight in Āśvina or Kārttika—on the preceding day, having performed his daily duties such as bathing and so forth, he should bathe [the deity] with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*): with curd for the heart, milk for the head, ghee for the crest-lock (*śikhā*), honey for the armor (*tanutra*), and sugar-candy for the eyes, along with *kuśa*-water. Then, having bathed [the deity] again with fragrant water and pure water using the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) as the means, [he should proceed].

Having placed sandalwood flowers and set them in pure vessels, he performs the sequential extraction; then, in the case of the *liṅga*, having placed the *liṅga* upon it, he worships it three times and fashions a lotus situated in the center of a yellow square, endowed with the eight jewels beginning with diamond.

It is endowed with eight medicinal herbs: uśīra, viṣṇukrāntā, red sandalwood, agallochum, śrīkhaṇḍa, sārikā, kuṣṭha, and śaṅkhinī; with eight metals: gold, copper, iron, tin, lead, brass, tin, and lead;
and with eight minerals: yellow orpiment, realgar, torikā, gold-oxide, mercury, cinnabar, red ochre, and sulphur.

Having prepared a golden vessel filled with fragrant water, accompanied by the eight grains—wheat, sesame, rice, mung beans, *yava*, wild rice (*nīvāra*), black rice (*śyāmāka*), and winter grains—and provided with flowers and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) since diamonds and other precious gems are unavailable; having fitted it with a conch-opening adorned with the sprouts of mango, *aśvattha*, banyan, *parkaṭī*, and *jambu* trees—or, in their absence, with a single sprout of mango and so forth—along with a vessel full of unbroken rice and a cord of white cloth as a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*); and having smeared it with sandalwood paste and placed it upon a fashioned lotus.

There, having meditated upon her as white, four-armed, seated in the lotus posture upon a white lotus, with the gesture of granting boons and a rosary in her right hands, and the vase of nectar and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands, adorned with white ornaments, graceful, and wearing a mass of matted hair and a crescent moon— (58b).

Having worshipped and satisfied [the deity] in three ways, and having offered incense, lamps, and so forth with this very [mantra]: *kā khā gā ghā ṅā hetukamahākṣetrapālāya saparivāreṇa saha baliṃ gṛhāṇa rakṣa rakṣa śāntiṃ kuru kuru svāhā* (5).
