In the same way, [offer] white [flowers]. 5 *Kṣā* to the one of terrifying form.
5 Having worshipped in the same manner, and having offered the *bali* with "5 *Kṣā* to the one of terrifying form" and so forth, [place them] in the *hetuka* jar and the subsequent jar.

In the same manner, [one should meditate on] the red-white [deity]. With "Oṃ, to the face of Brahmā," and so forth, having worshipped in that same way and offered the *bali* with "Oṃ, to the face of Brahmā," etc., [one should place it] in the northern jar relative to the jar situated in the southwest (*naiṛtya*). In the same manner, having meditated on the white-blue [deity] with five hoods, with "Āṃ, to Ananta," and so forth, having worshipped in that same way and offered the *bali* with "Āṃ, to Ananta," and so forth, thereafter, one should take flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and fragrance.
Whatever action has been commenced by me, whatever I shall do, and whatever has already been done—
may all that be rendered flawless through your command, O Hetuka.

Having thus requested permission individually from the presiding deities starting with Hetuka, and having uttered in a single sentence out of urgency, "Protect this sacrificial pavilion," one should place a water-pot there—

either to the north of the western pot or to the west of the northeastern pot— as before. Within that [pot], one should visualize the goddess who is red and fair, adorned with golden ornaments such as gems and finger-rings,
four-armed, three-eyed, and holding a lotus with its stalk, a boon-granting gesture, and a trident in her hands.
On her left, she holds a golden water-pot together with a lotus stalk, the *lajjā* (shame) plant, the *abhaya* (fearlessness) mudrā, and a cluster of jewels;
she is seated in the *padmāsana* posture upon a white lotus supported by various [auspicious] objects.
Having meditated on her filling the sacrificial pavilion (*makhamandapa*) with various divine jewels:

(62a) 5 *Śrīṃ*, for the sake of the glory of Sahā, *Śrīṃ* 5. Having worshipped as before with *Pā Pū*, one should prostrate; this is because there is no space [for the usual placement]. Even if the jars for Mṛtyuñjaya and others are not available, they should be placed in a linear sequence. Having prepared the maṇḍala and performed the *kumbhayāga* according to the stated procedure, one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) and so forth, after offering the fourfold oblation (*balicatuṣṭaya*) such as the *śānti* and others.

Having fashioned the mandalas of the four twilights and of the sun as if they were permanent, and having placed gold and other plaques upon them, one should prepare four twilight *argha* vessels, each filled with water and flowers and inscribed ten times with its respective seed-syllable (*bīja*). Having worshipped these and the Sun, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), one should prepare the deity’s *argha* vessel as usual and worship it with the root-mantra in the *sampuṭa* form, followed by the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) preceded by meditation.

Having arranged [the offerings] in the wind-corner in sequence, and having fashioned a mandala with six handfuls of water, one should place upon it a pedestal made of gold or other materials, topped with a lotus of six or eight petals. Having smeared it with the four-fold paste and meditated upon and worshipped the feet [of the deity] there, one should perform worship on the head as if it were the daily rite (*nityavat*) in the absence of a physical pedestal. Then, having worshipped the lineage of ordinary gurus in the fire-corner and the monthly guru in the southwest, and having performed the remaining worship according to the sequence—including the door-keepers, the scriptures, and the seats—and having worshipped the lineage of special gurus in the northeast, as well as Caṇḍa, one should again worship the two deities three times and receive the command (*ājñā*).

(63a) One should pray in the northeast or in the southeast. Due to the absence of a fixed location, one may also do so outside [the mandala], facing westward. Having performed the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), having fashioned a maṇḍala with *praṇavas*, and having placed upon it an arghya vessel containing water and flowers, [one should place] upon that—

5 kha ṭa 5 || 5 ka sa 5 || 5 ha gha 5 || 5 ra ya 5 || 5 ū 5 || 5 ā 5 || Having offered a flower with each of these [mantras], having placed the *tejīśakūṭa*, and having performed the installation of the fire as usual, one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) of three hundred and sixty or one hundred and eight sesame seeds smeared with clarified butter and consecrated by the *kāraṇa* [mantra]. Thereafter—having taken the *catrakas* (small sticks), one should sprinkle them ten times with the *tejīśakūṭa* using a single portion of the fire-offering water (*vahnyargha*). [Then] the *mṛtyuñjaya*...

Having placed [the vessel] near the jar, then having gone near the deity and worshipped the two deities three times, [one should offer] saffron and so forth. In the absence of these, one should offer them along with flowers in a leaf-cup made of *palāśa* or a cup made of mango leaves, as follows.
In the west: *Hnāṃ*, nine times; with *Kaṃkuma* [saffron], I perform the consecration (*adhivāsana*). *Hnāṃ*, five times. Likewise, in the north: with the *Śiras* mantra, musk; in the south:

with the *Śikhā* mantra, camphor; in the east: with the *Kavaca* mantra, sandalwood paste; in the center: with the *Netra* mantra, flowers along with scented water; in the northeast: with the *Astra* mantra, sugar. Again, having offered to the Deity ghee, honey, curd, and cooked rice mixed with the causal substances: *Hsphrāṃ*, obeisance to the Blessed One, Kamalā, *Hsphrāṃ*, to Samayā; with *Kaṃkuma*, I perform the consecration, five times.

(64a) Having likewise offered incense such as musk and the food offering (*naivedya*) with the remaining five-limbed mantras just as for the deity, and having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) with flowers accompanied by the appropriate causal [mantras] due to the absence of saffron and other substances, one should again worship the two deities three times.
Then, holding in one's joined palms (*añjali*) the four-fold perfume (*catuḥsama*) along with flowers and a perfumed sacred thread (*gandhapavitraka*), one should proceed.

"5. Oṃ, with [this] perfume and sacred thread (*pavitraka*), I worship the sandals of my Guru, the Lord Amukānandanātha, and his consort, the Mother Amukāparā. Having thus worshipped one's own Guru with the *pavitraka*, and having offered the sacred thread of perfume under the name of "Self-worship" (*ātmapūjā*) within oneself, then, by means of the root-mantra of the two deities, without [relying on] that specific authority. Thereafter...

In the twelve sections beginning with Mṛtyuñjaya, having offered scented pavitrakas with the mantra "I worship the sandals (*pādukā*) at the end of each respective mantra," and again, having applied the scented pavitrakas according to the sequence of occasional worship (*naimittika-pūjā*) as stated in the *Āgama* ending with the *bali*, thereafter, having performed the consecration (*adhivāsa*) starting from the *argha* offerings up to the seat (*āsana*), then, having placed the incensed scented pavitraka in the joined palms for the two deities: "Whatever merit has been offered by deed, mind, or speech, as long as the continuity [of existence] persists... [dehsraũ].
Hrīṃ, destroy! Hūṃ phaṭ!
May you become the supreme liberation for me; O you who rise above the duality of Brahman, be gracious through the thread of fragrance, O progenitor of all successions.

Having recited thus: *5 hrū̃ srū̃ 3 oṃ nrū̃ hrū̃ navātmānandanāthasamayāparā avvā 5*, and having offered the fragrant purifier (*gandhapavitraka*) once with the mantra *pā pū*, one should thereafter worship [the deities] from Aṣṭaka up to Caṇḍa according to the previously stated order of worship, using the fragrant purifier.
Then, having performed a magnificent great worship (*mahāpūjā*), sounding the bell and offering incense and lamps, and thereafter having presented the food offering (*naivedya*) and so forth;

then, having performed the fire sacrifice (*homa*) in the fire according to one's capacity, and if one has the capability, having performed its protection (*rakṣaṇa*), one should either recite [the mantra] or perform the dismissal (*visarjana*).

Thereafter, having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) and the offering of food for the virgins and others, one observing the vow should sleep. Regarding this consecration: at the end of each respective mantra, one should offer the *gandhapavitraka* (fragrant purifier) to all [the deities] using the mantra "I worship the *pādukā*," as well as the *bali*, the twilight rites (*sandhyā*), and everything up to the end of the *Caṇḍa* rite; this is the consecration. In the morning, having performed the bath and other rites, having entered the sacrificial pavilion (*yajñamaṇḍapa*), having performed the placement of the *praṇava* (*praṇavanyāsa*), and having performed the ritual bath with mantras (*mantrasnāna*), one should place the remaining water in another vessel.

Again, having performed the bathing mantra once more at that very spot, one should worship the specific and general gurus of the month with flowers moistened by that water. Having brought them into dissolution within one’s own guru, and thereafter having offered the *śānti* bali, one should worship each of the four junctions (*saṃdhyā*) and the sun with six handfuls of water and released flowers, one by one, using the water from their respective *argha* vessels.

Having offered the *arghya* water once and dismissed [the deities], and having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), one should worship and dismiss the feet, the deity’s *arghya* vessel, the two attendants, the seats of the [deities] and their arrival, the two deities, and Caṇḍa—each with water for the *arghya* and a flower, offering them once each. Having removed the floral remains (*nirmālya*) and separated the perfumes and sacred threads (*pavitraka*), one should place those floral remains, the food offerings (*naivedya*), and the perfumes and sacred threads in a secluded spot. Then, setting aside the dismissal of the jars dedicated to Mṛtyuñjaya and others, [one should take] their food offerings...

(66b) Having gone outside and performed the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*), one should place the Linga, which has been bathed, upon the *krama*. Having worshipped it three times with the root-mantra of the *saṃpuṭa*, one should again prepare the four *saṃdhyā* [offerings] for the Sun, Āgama, Argha, Dvāṣpa, Caṇḍacaraṇa, the Guru, and the General Guru, respectively, by forming thirteen mandalas; likewise, [one should offer] the golden band and so forth.

Having placed [the offering] upon that, and having performed the daily worship (*nityapūjā*) ending with Caṇḍa according to the stated sequence, thereafter, having completed the fire-oblation (*homa*), one should again perform the occasional (*naimittika*) worship ending with the *homa*. Then, having brought the sacred threads (*pavitraka*) near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should sprinkle them ten times with the water of the *argha* offering using the *tejīśakūṭa* mantra.

Having worshipped with the root-mantra of the two deities, one should offer that *pavitraka* beginning with the gurus as follows: in the northeast corner, one [flower] among twenty-one; a second among nine; a third among sixteen; and four among eighty-four. Thus, having worshipped each up to one’s own guru—one flower for each in their respective office—and in their absence:
*jū~ amukānandanāthāya gurave amukāparā avvā jū~ 5 akulakulakaulapavitrakeṇa pādukāḥ pūjayāmi* Having thus offered the *pavitraka*.

Having offered incense, flowers, incense-sticks, lamps, food offerings, and so forth, [he offers] the *pavitraka* again. Again, in the same manner, incense and so forth; again, the *pavitraka*; and again, having offered incense and so forth, he prostrates. Having placed the *pavitraka* upon himself, thereafter, he worships each of the twelve jars, such as the *mṛtyuñjaya*, according to the previously mentioned sequence, and likewise offers the *bali*.

Having worshipped with the *pavitraka*, and having again satisfied each [deity] individually with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and bali-offerings and libations (*tarpaṇa*), and having prostrated; then, having offered the fourfold bali together with the *pavitraka*, and thereafter, from the *sandhyā* rites up to the end of the *Caṇḍa* mantra, one should worship with the *pavitraka* at the end of each respective mantra, using the formula: "I worship the *pādukās* with the *pavitraka*.

Having again offered perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings to the two deities; having again offered a second *pavitraka*; again [offering] perfumes and so forth; again offering a third *pavitraka*;
and again offering perfumes and so forth—thereafter, having projected the descent of power (*śaktyavatāra*) by means of the *lambakrama* and having gratified the two deities, one goes near the fire.

Having projected the *pavitraka* for the fire solely with the ninefold self (*navātman*), and having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) according to one's capacity and offered it to the two deities, thereupon one performs the great worship (*mahāpūjā*).

(68b) Having performed an extensive celebration with incense, flowers, incense smoke, lamps, food offerings, and so forth, accompanied by dance, song, and instrumental music; having performed the eight-limbed prostration; having duly prepared the lamp and the *caru* oblation; having provided food for virgins and others; and having duly partaken of the lamp and the *caru* together with those of one’s own lineage; one should keep a vigil at night.
One should perform the offering of the purificatory thread (*pavitraka*) with the thought, "May [the deity] not depart.

Then, having bathed again at dawn and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *praṇava* as before, one should dismiss [the deity] according to the sequence for dismissing the fragrant purificatory thread. Having abandoned the circle of Caṇḍa, (69a)

Having constructed the twelve maṇḍalas according to the stated sequence, and having likewise worshipped the Deity up to the end of the *homa* according to the occasional (*naimittika*) procedure; then, having again performed the occasional worship up to the end of the *homa*, and having worshipped the Deity as before with the three *pavitrakas* accompanied by the descent of power (*śaktyavatāra*); then, having performed the *homa* according to one's capacity and offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, and having made the offering; one should construct the maṇḍala at the place of Caṇḍa as in the daily rite.
Saying "Aiṃ 5 Caṇḍāsanāya Aiṃ 5," one places a flower in the center of the mandala. Having uttered the syllable *Śrīṃ* over it and meditated upon Caṇḍa, one worships him three times.

Then, having offered to the two deities a sacred thread (*pavitraka*) preceded by perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth, one offers it to Caṇḍa. Next, having drawn forth four sacred threads for the two deities and thus performed the ritual installation (*samāropa*).

Having offered incense and the other articles in this sequence, and having placed the remaining three *pavitraka* threads [upon the deities], and having presented the accumulated food offerings (*naivedya*) and so forth, one should take a handful of flowers, kneel with hands and knees on the ground, and say: "By the grace of Kulacaṇḍa, the annual rite has been performed. May the fruit of this worship be complete for me; always fulfill my [desires]. Having spoken thus, one should offer a handful of flowers at the feet [of the deity] and prostrate. Then, having performed a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with his mantra according to one's ability, and having made the offering, one should again worship the two deities three times. One should also worship the general [deities], the monthly [deities], the Guru, and the four Lords of the Days (*ādinātha*).

Having performed the dissolution into one's own guru and having carried out the dismissal of the deities in the proper sequence; thereafter, having performed the dissolution of the twilight [deity] together with the sun of the fourfold [mantra] and having dismissed Kulacaṇḍa, one should offer five oblations with the *tejīśakūṭa* mantra and dismiss the fire.

O Lord, having dismissed the deities residing in the vessel [of the *mṛtyuñjaya*] with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), and having opened the sequence (*krama*), one should satisfy the deities of the sequence with the water from the *argha*-vessel using their respective mantras.

Lifting the *argha*-vessel, one offers the *arghya* to the Goddess with the *puṭa*-mantra. Having made the abode of the heart for the Goddess by means of the *yonimudrā*, and having drawn forth the jewel-flowers, one should erase the collection of lines with the *praṇavas*.

Having offered the *bali*—consisting of incense, thread, and purifying grass—at the place of the *abhivakṣya* and the *āsthāna-kṣetra*, and having performed the dismissal (*visarjana*); having specially worshipped the lineage of gurus (*gurupaṅkti*) and effected their dissolution (*laya*) into the Guru; having fully worshipped the Guru and likewise effected his dissolution; having worshipped the ground as usual; and having completed the daily worship (*nityapūjā*) with flowers; one should, by means of the water from the *mṛtyuñjaya* vessel, consecrate the *Navātman* within the water of the *Śrīghaṭa*.

Regarding the *pavitraka*: for one who is unable to perform it over three days, a *gandhasūtra-pavitraka* is prepared in a single day; however, on the following day, having performed the worship of the deity according to the prescribed sequence, one should likewise offer the *gandha-pavitraka* and so forth to Caṇḍa according to the ritual rules. In the case of the method of completion in a single day, after offering the *pūrṇāhuti* at the conclusion of the *gandha-pavitraka*, one should not dismiss the deity.

Having set aside Caṇḍa and removed the sacred threads (*gandhapavitraka*) from all [the deities], having placed them together in one spot, and having again applied the sacred threads in their proper order, and having waited for the duration of a *go* (or *yoha*) at the conclusion of the *pavipūrṇa*, having worshipped the Deity three times, thereafter, having offered a fragrant sacred thread to Caṇḍa, and having dismissed all the deities; in the case of a *liṅga*, having performed the daily worship (*nityapūjā*), and in its absence, having first performed the *indussa* [rite], he should satisfy the Guru to the best of his ability with gifts of gold, jewels, ornaments, garments, and sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) at the conclusion of the *śeka*.

(71b) One should perform the *saṃraṅga* [ritual]. The status of the annual worship (*varṣapūjā*) and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) is approved by the glorious Āgama. It was composed by the venerable Vimalaprabodha as a manual for the Pavitrārcana.
Now, the *dāmana* [ritual] is described; it is performed in the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra.
On the eighth and fourteenth days [for the practitioners], that which was spoken by Śambhu [is as follows]:
on the bright fortnight, the merit is a hundred-thousandfold; on the dark fortnight, it is a thousandfold;
and on the new moon day, it is declared by Śambhu to be half a hundred-thousandfold for those in the western region.
There, on the previous day, having performed the daily worship,
[he gathered] fruits and so forth, as much as could be held in a cow's ear, along with a complete collection of *damanaka* and *kadamba* flowers from the garden.

Having sprinkled [the site] with the group of six female messengers (*ṣaṭkadūtī*), worshipped them, and offered the *śānti* oblation, one should take one of the following vessels—gold, silver, copper, or a new earthenware vessel—and fill it with pure clay extracted by the *astra-mantra*. Into that, one should place a small *damanaka* plant; in its center, having produced several *damanaka* flowers from a fragrant *damanaka*, and in the center of those as well, having prepared the root, bark, wood, leaf, flower, and fruit of a single or double tree individually with the *astra-mantra*, one should establish each separately in the vessel with the *hṛdaya-mantra*. Therein, [one performs] the six-limbed [ritual] of the two deities.

Having performed the threefold placement in the sequence beginning from the root, and having provided them with flowers, one should place those *damanaka* sprouts— which were uprooted for the sake of the fragrant *damanaka*—
in their state as shoots for the purpose of the preparatory consecration (*adhivāsana*).

Thereafter, having uprooted the remaining cluster of *damanaka* plants with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should fashion clusters by wrapping them with thread according to the number of offerings— either one hundred and eight, half of that, half of that again (fifty-four), fifteen, ten, five, three, two, or one— and placing them in a vessel filled with clay from the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*). Having sprinkled them with the four-fold substances (*catuḥsama*) and so forth purified by the weapon-mantra,

consecrated them one hundred and eight times with the root-mantra (*mūla*), and fumigated them with incense using the root-mantra, one should cover them with a new cloth using the armor-mantra (*varman*) and worship them three times over the cloth with the root-mantra.
Having veiled [the vessel] with the *kavaca* mantra and protected it with the *astra* mantra, one should establish it.

Then, having performed the sequential extraction (*kramoddhāra*), and having placed the jar [therein] with the *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra, one should worship the Guru. Having requested permission, saying, "O Blessed One, I shall perform the *adamanaka-parvan*," one should dismiss [the deity].

Having placed *damanaka* wood trees in the eight directions of the sacrificial pavilion (*yajñamaṇḍapa*), and having established the ritual jars (*kumbha*) beginning with the *hetuka* and ending with the *śrīkumbha*, and having worshipped them according to the previous procedure; and having completed the occasional worship (*naimittikī pūjā*) up to the fire oblation (*homa*); [he should take] the four-fold mixture (*catuḥsama*) and the six items beginning with the root and ending with *damanaka*, as well as the *damanaka* sprouts that were set aside for the consecration (*adhivāsa*).

Having brought [the disciple] near the *kuṇḍa*, and having brought [the *damanaka*] near [him] with water for the *argha* offering along with perfumes and purifiers (*pavitraka*), he should double a single *damanaka* sprout together with the four-fold mixture (*catuḥsama*). [He should offer it] with:

*Jūṃ amukānandanāthagu(rave) amukāparā avvā jūṃ 5 sagandhadamanakena pā pū*. Having thus given it to the Guru, and in his own absence, having worshipped himself with perfumes and *damanaka* using the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*), he should worship the remainder according to the sequence of occasional worship (*naimittika-pūjā*) as described for the perfumes and purifiers, up to the seat of the Deity. Thereafter:
Having doubled unbroken grains of rice together with the four ingredients (*catuḥsama*) and sprouts of *damana* grass, and having fumigated them, one should place them in cupped hands (*añjali*).

Reciting the *saṃpuṭa-mantra*, one should worship the deity once: "Hrūā~ 5, I consecrate [this] for the ninefold self, Hrūā~ 5. To the west, [one should place] saffron and the root of *damana* grass mixed with musk.

With the *Mūrdha-mantra* on the south, [he places] sandalwood with camphor; with the *Śikhā-mantra* on the east, he places fragrant wood (*śrīvāsa*) with leaves; in the center, with the *Netra-mantra*, he places flowers with *hetu*; in the northeast, with the *Astra-mantra*, he places sugar with fruit. Thereafter, having offered to the deity ghee, honey, curd, and cooked rice accompanied by the *kāraṇa* [mantras]: "5 (Hsphrāṃ Na)mo Bhagavati Kamalāyi Hsphrāṃ Samayāyai Adhivāsayāmi 5. In this manner, having offered the remaining five limbs—[namely] the root-mantra and so forth—and in the absence of saffron and other substances, having performed the consecration (*adhivāsana*) even with flowers accompanied by *hetu*.

(74b) Furthermore, O gods, having worshipped [the deities] from the eight [Bhairavas] up to Caṇḍa in three ways with *gandhadamanaka*, and thereafter having performed a magnificent great worship (*mahāpūjā*), the remainder is as in the *pavitraka* rite; however, at the end of each respective mantra, one should worship the sandals (*pādukā*) with *gandhadamanaka*, saying: "I worship the sandals."

The term *yojanīyam* refers to the consecration (*adhivāsana*). Then, at dawn, having performed the ritual bathing and other preliminary rites, one should dismiss the deities from the sacrificial pavilion (*yajñamaṇḍapa*) according to the sequence of dismissing the perfumes and the sacred threads (*gandhapavitraka*). Subsequently, in accordance with that same procedure, one should perform the occasional rite (*naimittika*) and the daily worship (*nityapūjā*) ending with Caṇḍeśvara. Having completed the fire sacrifice (*homa*), one should again perform the occasional rite.

Having performed the worship ending with the *homa*, thereafter, one should bring the *damanaka* flowers, which have been gathered into a bunch, near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Having uprooted them with the *astra-mantra* and washed them with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should worship the two deities up to their seats according to the procedure for the *pavitraka*. Thereafter, having worshipped the two deities three times with *damanaka* using the root mantra, then: *Hrūāṃ Navātmānandanātha Hrūāṃ 5 damanakena pā pū*. In this same manner, having worshipped the Goddess with the remaining five limb-mantras: *Hsphrāṃ namo bhagavati kamalāyi Hsphrāṃ 5 samayāyai damanakena pā pū*.

(75b) Having worshipped the Goddess with the five-limbed mantras, one should then worship the deity three times at the end of the *saṃpuṭa* root mantra with: *hrīṃ rakṣa rakṣa hrīṃ*. Following that, [one should offer] the *damanaka* flower as the remainder of the sacred thread (*pavitraka*).

Again, having performed the bath at dawn, one should perform the dismissal (*visarjana*) in the same manner as before, preceded by the *praṇava-nyāsa* and following the sequence for the dismissal of the fragrant *pavitraka*. Likewise, having abandoned the [previous] mandala, one should construct the twelve mandalas according to the stated procedure. Having worshipped the deity up to the end of the fire-oblation (*homa*) according to the occasional (*naimittika*) rite, and having again performed the occasional worship up to the end of the *homa*, one should again perform the *homa* according to one's capacity. Having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and made the offering, one should construct the mandala as usual in the place of Caṇḍa: *aiṃ 5 caṇḍāsanāya aiṃ 5*.

(76a) Thus, having placed a flower in the center of the mandala, having uttered the syllable *Śrīṃ* over it, and having meditated upon Caṇḍa and performed worship three times; having offered to Caṇḍa for the two deities *gandha*, *damanaka*, and *damanaka*, preceded by perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings (*naivedya*), and having given the accumulated food offerings and so forth; one should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) with the mantra of Caṇḍa according to one's ability.
Having performed [the ritual] and offered the remainder as one does with the *pavitraka*, it is to be understood that this is the procedure for the *damanaka* [offering].

Now, the procedure for the *śayana-parvan* [the festival of the Lord’s sleep] is as follows: On the thirteenth day, having completed the daily obligatory rites and having extracted the ritual sequence (*krama*), one should install the *jaya-ghaṭa* [victory-pitcher], consecrated one hundred and eight times with the *amṛtyuñjaya-mantra*.

Having filled the *vardhanī* vessel with water scented with milk or with pure water, and having encircled the sacrificial pavilion (*yajñamaṇḍapa*) with an unbroken stream [of water] from all sides, one should place it near the jar (*ghaṭa*). After worshipping the Guru, one should request his permission, saying: "O Blessed Guru, I shall perform the rite for the propitiation of the two Śrī Navātman deities as previously described. Having thus requested permission and dismissed the Guru, one should install and worship the *hetukā* and other deities. Having performed the occasional worship (*naimittikī pūjā*), ending with the fire-oblation (*homa*), or even without the *homa*, one should pour the water from the *vardhanī* into separate vessels.

(77a) Having performed the libation for all [the deities] with that [liquor], and having placed the remainder of the libation from those vessels into a single vessel, he should offer the vessel, saying:
"O Śrī Kulacaṇḍavāsuki, be pleased by this vessel! Śrī! Thus, he offers the vessel.

Having prepared the lamp and the sacrificial rice (*caru*), and having used the substance contained in the *vardhanī* vessel for those two provided there is the capacity to do so—leaving aside the lamp and the *caru*—one should draw the mantra from the *vardhanī* with the heart-mantra of the deity and cause that substance to be given to the virgins and others. Thereafter, having performed the morning bath and other rites, and having dismissed [the deities] in the same manner, one should perform worship again; having worshipped them once more, one should consecrate the four-fold mixture (*catuḥsama*) for the two deities with the six limbs and offer it with the root-mantra of the two deities. One should cause the remainder to be given to Caṇḍa. Having prepared the lamp and the sacrificial rice...

(77b) Having provided a meal with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) for the young girls and others, having given a fee to the guru according to one's capacity, and having performed the *pūrṇāhuti* offering, one should dismiss [the deities] on that day or the following day. Sitting upon the bed, one should sprinkle oneself with the water from the jar using the *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra, recite the *saṃpuṭa-mantra* one hundred times, and half of that number of the *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra.
[The ritual for the festival of] lying down (*śayana*) is thus concluded.

Now, the rising (*utthāna*). On the fourteenth day of the rising festival, having performed his daily rites, the Guru should first prepare a mandala and satisfy [the deity] with gold and other offerings. Then he should say: "O Blessed One, I shall perform the rising festival.

Having received the command "ŪṂ JŪṂ SAḤ" five times, and having duly established the Mṛtyuñjaya and other vessels, performed the occasional worship (*naimittikī pūjā*), and brought near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) ten thousand, half that number, or even half of that— or as many as one is able— of *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice, and flowers, [he should treat them] like the sacred thread (*pavitraka*). Having placed the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra one hundred and eight times,
and having worshipped the Guru according to the lineage of gurus with five, three, or one flower each, as far as possible, he should then sacrifice himself.

Following the sequence of worship up to the end of the fire oblation (*homa*), one should then worship with flowers. Having filled eight hundred and eight handfuls of water and consecrated it with the three-syllable mantra (*tryakṣara*), one should offer it three times with the "enclosing" mantra (*saṃpuṭamantra*) of the two deities.

Again, having recited the enclosing mantra one hundred and eight times and performed the placement (*nyāsa*) one hundred and eight times, one should then place a garland of flowers. Then, having performed the fire oblation one hundred times for each of the [deities] along with the *śrīkhaṇḍa* [incense].

(Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*,) having presented the lamp and the sacrificial oblation (*caruka*), having performed the worship of the young girls (*kumārikā*) and others, and having utilized those two [the lamp and oblation], one should go outside, perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and re-enter.
Having recited the *Mṛtyuñjaya* mantra—a hundred and eight times for the purpose of protection—and having sprinkled oneself with the water from the deity’s *argha* vessel, [one should proceed].

Having filled another vessel with the fourfold [substances], [one offers] thirty-two [oblations] to the Goddess... [having removed the garland and given the remains to Caṇḍa]. Having dismissed [the deities] in due order and having smeared that [place] with the fourfold [substances], [placing the garland on one's head]. One should consecrate oneself with the water from the jar... [this is the ritual for the festival of rising].
(Now, the thirteenth chapter on the ritual procedure:

Having first performed the daily rites and worshipped the Guru preceded by the mandala, [one should worship] for the sake of attaining the fruit of worship and for the pleasure of Aśitāṅga-Mahābhairava, who is [present] in the moon.

I shall perform the *parva* [observance]. (Having requested [permission] and dismissed [the deities], having raised the sequence, having established the jars for Mṛtyuñjaya and others, and having performed the occasional worship, [one prepares] the tooth-cup mandala—the sequence—quadrangular, with a central circle marked by fourteen lotuses—in the northeast; *hsphreṃ* in the southwest; *hsrāṃ* in the northwest; and having offered a flower upon the pericarp. Likewise, the vessel for the [deceased] mandala, with flowers placed using the *praṇavas*...)

(Above that)—having placed [the syllable] *ka-pa-va* (only) together with the four flowers (*puṣpacatuḥsamasta*), having performed the ablution and having projected the moon three times, [one should] worship with the *praṇavas*. (80a) ...in the mandala, in the wind [direction]: *glauṃ* to Gaṇapati *glauṃ* 5. In the northeast: *hrīṃ* to Kulavaṭuka *hrīṃ* 5. In the southeast: *kṣauṃ* to Kṣetrapāla *kṣauṃ* 5.
In the southwest: *laḥ ceṭakāya laḥ* five times; having thus worshipped each with perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, and so forth, and having gratified them, then:
*hūṃ mahāpretāsanāya hūṃ* five times. Thus, having worshipped the seat in the four directions beginning with the east and in the center, [one offers]:
*aṃ ādigurunāthasthūlāyaparā avvā aṃ* five times, *pā pū*.
5 Aṃ Anādigurunātha-sūkṣmāparā Avvā Aṃ 5. 5 Ā Acintyagurunātha-susūkṣmāparā Avvā Aṃ 5. (80b)

(82b) The eleventh: On the new moon day of Śrāvaṇa, in the north: 5 yamayrū̃ madandhrīśamahābhairavanāthama(ho)cchuṣmāparā avvā aĩ yama(yrū̃ 5) pā (pū).
The twelfth [chapter]. These festivals (parvan) are to be performed like the first festival. 0. Now follows the rule for the festival of the first Guru:

on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, having performed one's daily rites, having received the command of the Guru, and having performed the occasional worship (naimittika-pūjā) preceded by the awakening of the jar (ghaṭajāga) and other rites, [one should draw] a square with the Praṇavas to the west of the deity.
Having fashioned a circular mandala one cubit in diameter, having created a sixteen-petaled lotus in its center and a nine-petaled lotus within that,

and having drawn four sets of eight-petaled lotuses in the four directions inside the constructed mandala; likewise, having offered five flowers with the *praṇavas*, and having prepared an *argha* mandala in front of that as before, one should place the *argha* vessel upon it.

In the same manner, having worshipped [the deity] and having sacrificed to the quartet beginning with Gaṇa, having worshipped the seat, and having worshipped the quartet of gurus beginning with Ta-tādi in the four lotuses starting from the east, [one worships] in the center: Jūṃ 5. Having worshipped three times the Kali-guru who is joined with the Aṅgas, Candra-śakti, and Ciñciṇī-nātha: Jūṃ 5 Pā Pū. 5 Śrī Gaganānandanātha 5 Pā Pū.

5 Śrī Kumudānandanātha, 5 Pā pū. 5 Śrī (Padmānanda)nātha, 5 Pā pū. 5 Śrī Bhairavānandanātha, 5 Śrī Devānandanātha, 5 Śrī Kamalānandanātha, 5 Śrī Śivānandanātha, 5 Śrī Rāmānandanātha, 5 Śrī Kṛṣṇānandanātha, 5. These [are worshipped] on the nine petals.
5 Śrī Candrapuranātha, 5. 5 Śrī Gulmanātha, 5. 5 Śrī Stambhanātha, 5. 5 Śrī Kārppāśanātha, 5. 5 Śrī Vaṭapuranātha, 5.

(84a) 5 Śrī Virajanātha 5 । 5 Śrī Prabhāsanātha 5 । 5 Śrī Bhogapuranātha 5 । 5 Śrī Bimbadevīnātha 5 । 5 Śrī Khaḍganātha 5 । 5 Śrī Rudranātha 5 । 5 Śrī Dhārāśivanātha 5 । 5 Śrī Mudrāsphoṭanātha 5 । 5 Śrī Vaṅkāpuranātha 5 । 5 Śrī Bhojyadevanātha 5 ।

Having worshipped these [deities] on the sixteen petals with perfumes, flowers, and so forth—provided there is the capacity—the eighty-four gurus should be worshipped. Following that, having worshipped the two deities, prepared the lamp and the sacrificial offering (*caruka*), and worshipped the circle (*cakra*) beginning with the young girls, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the guru according to one's ability. Then, one should perform the consumption of the lamp and the sacrificial offering.

Having offered the *argha* in the same sequence as before, one should perform the dismissal (*visarjana*) in that very same manner; such is the procedure for the thirteen festivals. According to another tradition, there are eighteen festivals together with Śiva, Sadāśiva, Durvāsas, Mīnanātha, and Śrīkaṇṭhanātha. Now follows the ritual procedure for the Great Festival (*mahāparva*).

This is the procedure for one who is capable of performing thirteen joints (*parva*) individually. On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, having performed the daily rites and having gratified the Guru with gold and other offerings within the previously established mandala, one should take the command [with the mantra]: *Jūṃ! O Guru, son of Amuka, I shall perform this joint-filling, the thirteenth joint; Jūṃ!* (85a)

Having raised the sequence [of lines] at intervals of two finger-breadths in the eight directions, one should construct two mandalas in the east: a square [mandala] with the *praṇavas* and a circle five finger-breadths in diameter in the center. One [mandala] in the southeast, two in the south, one in the southwest, three in the west, one in the northwest, two in the north, and one in the northeast. Having thus fashioned these thirteen mandalas, having offered flowers upon each mandala with the respective *praṇavas*, having provided the seat as before, and having established the jars for Mṛtyuñjaya and the others according to the occasional (*naimittika*) procedure.

Having worshipped [the deity] ending with Sūrya and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), one should place the *argha* vessel before the sequence. Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the deities of the lineage, on that day or in the corner, there is no worship of the feet. Having worshipped the feet as in the daily rite, if there is authority [to do so], one should worship at the head of the special row; otherwise, having worshipped the Guru, one does the same for the Lord of Devas (*Deveśāna*).

There is no worship even for the Guru. Then, having offered the five-fold bali of pacification and so forth at the northeast corner or the north of the Krama, one should place a flower upon the Krama with the five *praṇavas*. Thereafter, having performed the worship of the deities in their proper order up to Caṇḍa, [one places the substances] to the east of the deity:
*haṃ* five times, red sandalwood; in the southeast: *saṃ* five times, vermilion; in the south: *kṣaṃ* five times, musk; in the southwest: *maṃ* five times, cardamom.
In the west: *laṃ* five times, camphor; in the northwest: *vaṃ* five times, a red lotus; in the north: *ya* five times, barley flowers; in the northeast: *rā* five times, fragrance.

Thereafter, filling both hands with all these along with flowers, one should offer them to the two deities while reciting the *saṃpuṭa* mantra. Then, in the thirteen mandalas starting from the east...

Having worshipped the [deities] ending with Ciñciṇī with perfumes and other offerings; having prostrated to the two deities; having offered perfumes and so forth; having performed the recitation (*japa*) and made the offering; having presented the great oblation (*mahābali*);

having performed the fire sacrifice (*homa*) and made the offering; and having removed the great oblation and cast it in the cardinal and intermediate directions—having thus become pure, one should sleep. This is the consecration (*adhivāsana*). (86b)

Having performed the morning ablutions and so forth, having performed the dismissal according to the stated sequence, and having completed the daily rites according to the occasional (naimittika) procedure, one should again perform the occasional worship. Having prepared the sacrificial pap (*caruka*) for the month of Kārttika, one should offer it to each of all [the deities] together with their vessels. Having performed the recitation (*jāpya*), one should present it to the two deities. Following that, taking the vessel filled with fragrant substances: *Hraḥ rkṣraḥ aṃ, O Lord of all festivals, grant me success and accomplishment!* Having given this to the deity and having given the ritual fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Guru, [one should give it] to the young girls and others.

Having performed the great worship (*mahāpūjā*), having utilized the lamp and the sacrificial rice offering (*caruka*), and having sipped water for purification (*ācamana*), one should perform the worship of Caṇḍa either at the end of that same day or on another day, and then carry out the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*).
This is the procedure for the Great Festival (*mahāparvavidhi*).

Now, whether one's own guru is living or deceased, one should perform the *siddhaparva* rite as follows: having completed the daily rites on the anniversary of one's own initiation; having performed the occasional (*naimittika*) worship preceded by the extraction of the lineage (*kramoddhāra*); having placed a water-pot (*kalaśa*) again as before in the northeast corner of the deity's shrine; having worshipped Mṛtyuñjaya there according to the rules; and having worshipped the two deities (or the triad) again; having prepared the lamp and the sacrificial rice (*caru*); and having drawn a mandala in front of the manifest guru, one should worship the guru with the *pūrṇāhuti* offerings and other rites.

Having had [the disciple] eat by the hand of the Guru and having sprinkled himself with the water from the *mṛtyuñjaya* jar, if the Guru is staying in another land, one should construct a mandala, worship the Guru,
and perform the consecration with one’s own hand. Following that, having performed the worship of the virgins and others, and having made use of the lamp and the *caru*, one should dismiss the deity.

In the absence of a *kalaśa* (vase), it is prescribed that the worship of Mṛtyuñjaya be performed in a vessel for the sixfold *arghya*. Regarding the option of using clay: at dawn on an auspicious day, one should take hold of the feet of the Guru or someone born of his lineage; or, in the absence of all these, before the deity of the *Krama-āgama*, having prepared a mandala with fragrant substances. Then, having addressed [the deity] with this formula: "Hrūṃ! O Amuka-Bhairava, O Amuka-Bhairavī, for the sake of attaining the power of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*), I perform the *parvan* today; grant me your command! (Hrūṃ). Thus, one should invoke them.

(88a) Then, having sprinkled [the vessel] with the *nūtanapātra* mantra and washed it with the *hṛdaya* [mantra], and having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *mṛtyujaya-aṇu*, one should fully prepare the materials such as rice and so forth. Having kindled the new fire with the gaze of the two deities, one should complete the cooking with the *astra* [mantra]. Alternatively, having looked upon the food prepared by ordinary people with the gaze of the two deities, [one should consecrate it] with the divine *astra* [mantra].

Having sprinkled [the area] with water consecrated by the *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra one hundred and eight times; having drawn a mandala with *praṇavas* and placed the cooking vessel upon it; having protected it with the *astra* mantra; then, in the northeast corner of the courtyard crowded with initiated persons—or, in the case of uninitiated persons, having prepared a cubit-sized mandala in the middle of the house with cow dung using *praṇavas*.

Having offered the seat with the mantra "ŪṂ JŪṂ, obeisance to all beings and animals," and having washed the feet of the preceptor seated there, performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) with *praṇavas*, and prepared the *argha* mandala like that of one's own guru-mandala, one should prostrate, smell the flower, and discard it. Thereafter, having fashioned a square mandala measuring one cubit and a circle in its center using fragrant substances and so forth, one should worship the four primary lineage gurus from the east to the north within that [circle]. Then, having meditated upon the form of the deity in the center—

Having worshipped [the deity] in three ways, and then having worshipped the group of four beginning with Gaṇeśa from the northwest to the southwest, and having circumambulated [the deity], the food and so forth, together with its cause, should not be recited over while being placed in another vessel.
(89b) Not to be recited (90a)

Having dismissed [the deities] and worshipped one’s own guru, the fruit of that [practice] accrues to you for the sake of performing the remaining rites of the daily observance (nityavrata). Alternatively, having performed the worship ending with Caṇḍa, and having again worshipped the two deities three times, one should recite the "enclosing" (saṃpuṭa) mantra one hundred and eight times. Having offered it to the deity with the previous formula, and having recited the twenty-four verses beginning with Aṭṭahāsa and ending with Rājagṛha, one should prostrate. The fruit of that [practice] accrues for the sake of performing the remaining rites of the daily observance.
The occasional rite has been indicated in the *Paścimārcanapaddhati* by the venerable Vimalaprabodha, both in brief and in detail.
This concludes the second procedure, composed by the venerable Vimalaprabodha, the teacher of the six lineages (*ṣaḍanvaya*) and a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) of the supreme haṃsa order. 0.
The sequential extraction (kramoddhāra) should be performed for the omitted sections among the unspoken parvans;

it is also described here in whatever manner is necessary for the accomplishment of one's desired goal. Having completed the daily rites, having prepared the five mandalas of the two deities as usual, having placed the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) upon the mandala of the scriptures, and having placed the auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha) within the mandala of the deity.

Having prepared the *argha* vessel, performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the deity, worshipped the feet [of the deity] and the Guru, offered the fourfold oblation (*bali*) for peace and so forth, and performed the worship of the gatekeepers and the [deities of the] scriptures;

[one should prepare] a vessel made of gold, silver, or bell-metal—either one of these being the material. The best is thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in size, the middling is twenty-eight finger-breadths, the inferior is twenty-five finger-breadths, and the lowest of the low is the measure of a single cubit (*ratni*).

[One should take] a most inferior [substance] held in the hand of a shaven-headed person, who has fasted; it should be placed in a bell-metal vessel, purified by bathing with pure ashes, and washed with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) of the Goddess. Having established it upon an auspicious seat (*bhadrapīṭha*) with the *praṇavas*, and having smeared it with the four ingredients (*catuḥsama*) using the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), one should cast vermilion (*sindūra*) from the head onto it while it remains within a cloth. Then, according to the desired purpose, [one should use] a three-finger-long gold rod ending in a swastika.

Having taken [the water] with the *śikhā* [finger], having washed it, having worshipped it with the *kavaca*, and having saluted it with the *dṛś* [finger]: in a peaceful rite (*saumyakarman*), [one should apply it] primarily with the ring finger and thumb;

in a fierce rite (*ugrakarman*), having opened [the hand] with the middle finger, thumb, and index finger; in between, according to the vessel. Having applied six drops in the sequence of a circle—starting from the north-east (water), wind, east, fire, and south-west—with the mantra: *glūṃ slūṃ mlūṃ plūṃ nlūṃ hsauṃ hsauṃ hsauṃ*, [one should proceed]. Having written the seed-syllables of the twenty-eight mandalas in sequence—*kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ caṃ* in the southeast; *chaṃ* in the south; *jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ* in the southwest; *ḍhaṃ* in the west; *ṇaṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ* in the northwest; *paṃ* in the north; *phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ yaṃ raṃ* in the northeast; and *laṃ* [in the center]—then, in the southeast corner, below the syllable *chaṃ*, write *aiṃ hsaḥ aiṃ*; and in the southwest, below the syllable *ṭaṃ*.
